## [30+ International School Interview Questions 2026](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/international-school-interview-questions/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/international-school-interview-questions/  
**Date:** 2026-06-23

23 June 2026 Ozlem Cimen 12 min read Updated: 3 October 2026 Summary Real questions asked in Dubai and UAE international school interviews — by age group for students, plus parent meeting questions — with guidance on what to say and what to avoid. 
# 30+ Real International School Interview Questions 2026: Child & Parent
Quick Answer — What Gets Asked in Interviews? Children: "Tell me about yourself", "What's your favourite subject?", "How does it feel to be somewhere new?" Parents: "How would you describe your child's learning style?", "Why did you choose this school?" Dubai and UAE interviews are placement-focused, not elimination-focused — honest, natural answers beat rehearsed scripts every time. We have another guide covering the general interview preparation framework — a 4-phase, 30-day plan including the parent meeting. This article is its companion: the actual questions that get asked. I have accompanied families to dozens of interviews in Dubai and the UAE; the questions below are drawn directly from those experiences. You cannot memorise every possible question, but knowing the most common ones significantly boosts both your child's and your own confidence. Remember: International school interviews in Dubai and the UAE are placement -focused, not elimination-focused. The school is asking questions to understand which year group and which programme your child fits best — not to reject them. Knowing this difference is itself a major form of preparation. 
## Primary School (Ages 5–10) — Child Questions
At this age, questions are deliberately kept simple and social. The school is not measuring academic performance — it is observing your child's ability to communicate, express themselves, and demonstrate social maturity. "Tell me about yourself. What's your name, how old are you, tell me something about your family." Why it's asked: To see whether the child can speak comfortably and spontaneously. The ideal answer is short, natural and in their own words — even "My name is Elif, I'm 8, I have two brothers" is perfectly sufficient. "What do you enjoy most outside school?" Why it's asked: To understand interests and areas of passion — the school may use this to suggest clubs, sports or activities when placing your child. There is no right or wrong answer. "How does it feel to be somewhere new?" Why it's asked: To gauge adaptation capacity. A child saying "scary but exciting" or "a bit hard but I'll get used to it" is far more convincing than a rehearsed "very happy." "Has there ever been a time at school when you found something hard? What did you do?" Why it's asked: To understand how the child responds to difficulty. Saying "I asked for help / I tried again / I asked my teacher" paints a strong profile. "What do you do if you disagree with your best friend?" Why it's asked: To assess conflict resolution style and empathy. A simple answer like "We talk and try to sort it out" meets expectations well. 
## Middle School (Ages 11–14) — Child Questions
At this age, questions become more analytical and personal. The school is trying to measure how your child thinks, their self-awareness, and their social consciousness. "If you could change the world for one day, what would you do?" This question is not random — the school is looking for alignment between its values and how your child sees the world. What matters is not a "correct" answer but a personal, defensible one. "I'd make sure everyone has clean water, because..." is simple but genuine, and it works. "Which subject feels most like you? Why?" Self-awareness is being tested, not academic strength. "Science, because it chases the why and how" or "Literature, because I get to see different perspectives" — these are strong, original answers. "Do you prefer teamwork or working alone? Why?" There is no wrong answer. The school wants to hear that your child is aware of their preference and can also adapt to the alternative. A nuanced answer like "I can usually do both, but I tend to..." feels more authentic. "Is there something specific you want to learn at this school?" Researching the school's programme in advance and naming something specific — "I saw you have a robotics club, I'd really like to try that" — distinguishes your child's application from others. 
## Secondary School (Ages 15–18) — Child Questions
At this level, the school wants to understand your child's career vision, the motivation behind their curriculum choice, and their global awareness. Questions are deeper. "Why do you want to do IB / A-Level / AP specifically?" "Because it's prestigious" or "my parents wanted it" are answers to avoid. A strong answer: "I researched that IB provides a strong foundation for applying to universities outside Turkey; I'm genuinely interested in the independent study components like the Extended Essay." Specific, researched, authentic. "Pick a global issue and explain what could be done about it." A favourite at IB schools. The topic itself matters less than whether your child can see an issue from multiple angles. Single-track solutions versus "on one hand... on the other..." framing shows more mature thinking. "What is your biggest challenge and how do you manage it?" Although it looks like a weakness question, it measures self-awareness and a growth mindset. "I struggle with stress management but I've recently started..." is far stronger than "everything's fine, no challenges." "Why did you choose this school and how do you want to contribute here?" A two-part question confirming both that your child has researched the school and that they want to participate actively. Answering with a concrete plan — "I'd like to join the debate club and..." — is effective. Ozlem Cimen — Coach's note The best interview preparation is not question-and-answer drilling — it's talking through these questions with your child at the dinner table in a relaxed way. When you ask "What's hardest for you?" or "What do you like and not like about school?" your child is preparing, and you as a parent are understanding their perspective more deeply. That second gain lasts much longer than the interview itself. 
## Parent Meeting: Questions the School Actually Asks
The parent meeting typically lasts 15–30 minutes, either alongside or immediately after the child's assessment. The school's goal is not to evaluate you — it is to understand your child better and see whether your family's values align with the school's. "How would you describe your child's learning style?" Academic strengths and weaknesses are not what's being asked — it's about how they learn. Observations like "visual learner," "learns by doing," or "keeps asking questions until they fully understand" are very useful. "What challenges did they face at their previous school?" Be honest. Problems that are concealed tend to surface during the assessment or in the first few weeks. The school needs to know what to look out for — they don't want surprises. "Why did you choose this school?" Avoid "great reputation" or "everyone sends their children here." Prepare an answer that highlights a specific feature, programme or approach you researched. "What is your family's approach to education?" The school wants to understand how involved and supportive the family is. Answers that show balance — "we help with homework but let our child make their own decisions" — are strong. "Is there anything else you'd like us to know about your child?" Don't leave this blank. It's your opportunity to speak — use it to highlight a strength, a growth area, or a specific circumstance about your child. 
## Most Common Interview Mistakes
Parents steering the child's answers: Intervening in the interview room shows parental anxiety, not the child's confidence. The admissions team always notices. Presenting everything as perfect: "We had no difficulties, everything was wonderful" does not build trust. Schools prefer a realistic, growth-focused picture. Name-dropping other schools: Mentioning "we also applied to GEMS Wellington" is not always well-received by admissions teams. Focus: why is this school right for you? Over-rehearsing your child: Memorised answers are spotted immediately. IB schools in particular are assessing independent thinking — originality, not formula, is what's measured. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### What kinds of questions are asked in international school interviews?
Questions vary by age: primary-level interviews focus on social and personal questions; middle school adds analytical thinking; secondary school questions assess career vision and global awareness. 
### What do schools ask at the parent meeting?
Common parent questions: your child's learning style, challenges at the previous school, why you chose this school, and your family's approach to education. 
### Can a child with limited English attend an international school interview?
Yes — they go through an EAL (English as an Additional Language) assessment instead. Limited English is not a reason for rejection; it informs the support plan the school creates for your child. 
### How much preparation time is needed for the interview?
2–3 weeks of natural, relaxed conversation for 20–30 minutes a day is sufficient. The goal is not memorisation — it is helping your child feel comfortable expressing themselves. 
### What should we do if the interview is unsuccessful?
Request feedback from the school, ask to be placed on the waiting list, and look at alternative schools with a good profile match for your child. # How Does a Child with Limited English Adapt to a Dubai School?
Summary Children with limited English successfully adapt to Dubai's international schools every day. What are EAL programmes, how does the adaptation timeline vary by age, what questions should you ask, and what can you do at home? You've decided to move to Dubai. Visas are sorted, a home has been found, work is arranged. But there's a question circling relentlessly in the back of your mind: "My child has had some English at school in Turkey, but not enough. What's going to happen in Dubai?" I hear this from many families. Most children in Turkey receive some school English — but that English is usually not sufficient to use as a daily medium of instruction in an international school in Dubai. A close friend's son faced exactly this situation: he had a few years of school English behind him, but in those first weeks he simply couldn't find his way into the fluent conversations happening all around him in class. Looking back now, I can say clearly: most of what I worried about was unnecessary. But the parts I was caught unprepared for were genuinely difficult. This post is here to map that difficulty for you in advance. Ozlem Cimen — A note from your coach My son arrived in Dubai with virtually no classroom English. The first months were hard. But within a year he was speaking fluently. I'm sharing everything I learned from that experience here. 
## Let's Be Honest First: Yes, the Start Is Hard
I won't sugarcoat it. The first few months will not be easy for your child. Sitting in class without understanding, struggling to break into the social group, not fully grasping what the teacher is asking — these are real difficulties. But I also need to say this: Dubai schools face this situation every single day. Because the vast majority of students in Dubai come from families whose first language isn't English. Schools know this reality and are structured accordingly. 
## How Do Dubai Schools Provide Support?
International schools in Dubai run specialist programmes called EAL (English as an Additional Language) or ELL (English Language Learners). These programmes are designed precisely for a child in your situation. An assessment is done at enrolment. The school measures your child's English level during the application process. For younger children this is usually play-based; for older students more systematic tests are used. The point isn't to screen children out — it's to understand how much support they'll need. An individual language plan is prepared. Well-established schools like GEMS Royal Dubai School create an Individual Language Development Plan for each student with limited English. This plan sets out which targets will be tracked across the term. The EAL teacher enters the classroom. In some schools the support teacher doesn't only see your child in a separate room — they're present during science, maths and other lessons too, using translator apps and visual tools to bridge comprehension gaps. Peer integration is prioritised. As one EAL coordinator put it: "These children are not cognitively lacking. They're on a language journey. Research shows they go on to genuinely outperform over time." 
## How Long Does Adaptation Take?
The honest answer: it varies by age and the child's character. Children aged 4–8 adapt the fastest. Language acquisition at this age is almost a biological reflex. I've seen many children communicating comfortably with peers within 6–12 months. Ages 9–12 may take a little longer — 12–18 months. But in this group too, academic performance typically recovers rapidly once language develops. 13 and above is the most challenging group. Entering a new environment during a critical period for both language and identity development is complex. For this age group, school selection needs to be particularly careful — schools with strong EAL programmes and a genuine focus on social integration should be prioritised. 
## Questions to Ask When Choosing a School
Every Dubai school says it offers EAL support. But the quality varies enormously. Ask these directly during visits or calls: "How does your EAL/ELL programme work?" A general answer isn't enough. How many EAL teachers do you have, how long does the programme run, do you offer in-class support or only separate sessions — get specific. "How long does adaptation typically take for children in similar situations?" Critical for realistic expectation management. "How will you communicate with my child in the first month?" Some schools match new students with a buddy who shares their home language. This small detail makes the first weeks much easier. "How often do you give parents progress feedback?" Good schools update monthly, some even fortnightly. 
## What You Can Do at Home
Even with school support, the home environment is decisive. Bring English into daily life. Switch from Turkish dubbing to English audio with Turkish subtitles on Netflix. Your child will resist at first — but their ear begins to adjust. Convert school English into living English — before you move. If you can start 2–3 months before relocating, build English habits outside school hours. Using words they already know in real contexts — writing a shopping list, playing an English game, watching a simple series — turns classroom English into a living language. They're not starting from zero; they need activation. Don't push, observe. When your child comes home, instead of "what did you learn today, could you speak English?" ask how they're feeling, who they sat next to, what they had for lunch. Social adaptation comes before language adaptation. Don't neglect Turkish. You don't have to lose one language while learning another. Children raised bilingually have higher cognitive flexibility. Keep Turkish alive at home — school will take care of the English. 
## Be Wary of Schools Without Real EAL Programmes
Some schools in Dubai say "we accept everyone" but have no genuine EAL infrastructure. In that case your child may spend days sitting in class without understanding anything — creating both academic and psychological burden. KHDA inspection reports include assessments of each school's EAL/ELL support. Review these reports before school visits. Schools rated "Outstanding" or "Very Good" typically offer this support more systematically. 
## Conclusion: Decide from Knowledge, Not Fear
Children with limited English successfully adapt to Dubai schools every day. Two things are required: the right school and an informed family. Finding the right school — matched to your child's age, character and needs — is exactly what Edualist does. I have witnessed hundreds of expat families navigate this process, and in every single case the most critical difference came from the preparation made in choosing the school . If you're asking "where do I start?" — reach out. Let's arrange a free consultation. Author Ozlem Cimen International education consultant and founder of Edualist. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can a child with limited English be accepted to a Dubai school?
Yes. The vast majority of international schools in Dubai accept students with limited English through EAL/ELL programmes. A level assessment is done before enrolment and a support plan is prepared accordingly. 
### Are schools with EAL programmes more expensive?
EAL support is generally included in the school fee. Some schools may charge extra for intensive individual support — clarify this before enrolment. 
### What age is easiest for language adaptation?
Ages 4–8 is the fastest period for language acquisition. But adaptation is possible at any age — the timeline and level of support needed simply varies. 
### What happens if my child can't adapt?
A school with a good EAL programme tracks progress regularly and intensifies support when needed. If the school doesn't offer this flexibility, it's a sign the school choice needs to be reconsidered. 
### Can Turkish and English be learned at the same time?
Absolutely. Growing up bilingual is not a disadvantage — it's a cognitive advantage. Preserving Turkish at home does not hinder your child's English learning; on the contrary, a strong mother tongue foundation facilitates new language acquisition.

## [My Child's Character Strengths: 24 VIA Examples](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/my-childs-character-strengths/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/my-childs-character-strengths/  
**Date:** 2026-10-11

Character strengths VIA framework Child assessment Child development School forms When parents ask "what are my child's strengths?", the first answers that surface are usually vague: "she's good at maths" or "he's very curious." But how reliable are these observations — and which qualities represent your child's deepest, most enduring strengths, independent of grades, teacher comments, or any given day's performance? This guide focuses on your child's character strengths — the personality traits that make them who they are. Our framework is the VIA (Values in Action) Character Strengths model, used by over 15 million people in 190+ countries and developed by positive psychology pioneers Martin Seligman and Christopher Peterson. In this guide: What character strengths are and how they differ from cognitive strengths · The VIA's 6 virtues · How each of the 24 strengths shows up in children · Three ways to discover your child's signature strengths · Ready-to-use phrases for school forms · How character and cognitive profiles complement each other 
## What Is a Character Strength?
Character strengths are the positive personality traits that feel most natural to a person — the qualities they express consistently, often with little effort, across different situations. The VIA framework identifies 24 of these traits, grouped under 6 core virtues shared across cultures worldwide. Character strengths are a separate dimension from cognitive strengths. A cognitive profile shows "how your child thinks" — verbal, numerical, and spatial reasoning capacity. A character profile shows "who your child is" — traits like curiosity, perseverance, empathy, and integrity. Together they form a child's complete portrait. Research finding: Angela Duckworth's landmark studies found that grit — a combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals — predicts academic and career success more powerfully than IQ. Character strengths reveal what grades cannot. Looking for cognitive strengths? If you're interested in your child's verbal, numerical, and spatial reasoning capacity, see our companion guide: Your Child's Strengths & Weaknesses: Cognitive Profile & Assessment Guide → 
## The VIA Framework: 6 Virtues and 24 Character Strengths
The VIA framework groups the 24 character strengths under 6 core virtues. Each virtue contains 3–5 related strengths. Your child's "signature strengths" — their most dominant 5 traits — emerge from within these 24. 🔍 Wisdom Strengths related to acquiring and applying knowledge: Creativity, Curiosity, Judgement, Love of Learning, Perspective. 🦁 Courage Strengths for reaching goals despite obstacles: Bravery, Perseverance, Honesty, Zest. ❤️ Humanity Strengths in caring relationships with others: Love, Kindness, Social Intelligence. ⚖️ Justice Strengths related to community and civic life: Teamwork, Fairness, Leadership. 🧘 Temperance Strengths that protect against excess: Forgiveness, Humility, Prudence, Self-Regulation. ✨ Transcendence Strengths that connect to meaning beyond the self: Appreciation of Beauty, Gratitude, Hope, Humour, Spirituality. 
## All 24 Strengths: How They Appear in Children
Every strength has its own signature in children. Below, each one is described in terms of observable behaviour. Tick the ones you see consistently in your child — the 5 you tick most often point to their signature strengths. 
### Wisdom
Creativity: Generates original ideas in play, drawing, and problem-solving; actively looks for new ways to approach familiar tasks. Curiosity: Asks endless "why?" and "how?" questions; explores topics they find interesting without being prompted. Judgement (Critical Thinking): Weighs different perspectives before deciding; not easily swayed by "everyone does it this way" — they look for evidence and reasons. Love of Learning: Enjoys acquiring new knowledge for its own sake, whatever the topic; seeks to go deeper even outside school. Perspective: Sees situations in a broader context; makes observations that seem mature for their age and can hold a real conversation with adults. 
### Courage
Bravery: Doesn't avoid difficult situations; speaks up when they believe something is right, even under pressure. Perseverance: Doesn't give up once they've started something; obstacles slow them down but don't stop them. Honesty: Tells the truth even when it's hard; what they say matches what they do; no performance, just themselves. Zest: Approaches life with energy and enthusiasm; gives full attention and effort to what they're doing. 
### Humanity
Love: Nurtures close relationships with care; warmth and affection come naturally and genuinely. Kindness: Gets genuine satisfaction from helping others; looks for opportunities to assist without being asked. Social Intelligence: Reads the emotional atmosphere in a room quickly; has an intuitive sense of how to approach different people. 
### Justice
Teamwork: Puts the group's success above personal gain; genuinely prefers winning together to winning alone. Fairness: Strong sense of "that's not fair"; advocates for rules applied equally to everyone; dislikes favouritism. Leadership: Organises groups naturally; works to include everyone in the process and is uncomfortable when someone is left out. 
### Temperance
Forgiveness: Doesn't carry grudges; prefers to repair a relationship over seeking revenge. Humility: Doesn't inflate achievements; notices and acknowledges others' contributions and qualities. Prudence: Thinks before acting; considers the consequences of choices in advance; avoids decisions they'll regret. Self-Regulation: Can manage emotions and impulses; able to say no; can brake before reacting. 
### Transcendence
Appreciation of Beauty: Genuinely moved by music, art, nature, or a perfectly written sentence; has frequent "wow" moments. Gratitude: Notices and remembers the good things others do; says thank you without being prompted. Hope: Maintains an optimistic view of the future; says "it'll get better" in hard moments — and means it. Humour: Enjoys making others laugh; uses humour to ease tension; finds the lighter side of situations. Spirituality: Interested in questions of meaning and purpose; genuinely asks "why are we here?" and "what's the point of it all?"

Signature strengths — a child's most dominant 3–5 character traits — emerge most reliably when three methods are combined: 
### Three Discovery Methods

Context diversity Play, school, family, friends — traits that appear consistently across multiple contexts are genuine strengths. A quality that only shows up in one setting may be a context effect, not a core trait. 3. School registration forms, student profile reports, and admission interviews frequently ask: "What are your child's strengths?" Replace generic answers with character-specific, concrete phrases. The ready-made examples below can be used directly: He is genuinely curious — he researches topics that interest him without prompting and goes well beyond what the curriculum covers. She is highly perseverant — when she faces a setback she doesn't give up; she tries different approaches until she reaches her goal. He is deeply honest — what he says matches what he does, and he tells the truth even when it's uncomfortable. She shows strong empathy — she quickly notices how others around her are feeling and looks for ways to help. He is a natural team player — he puts group success above personal recognition and genuinely prefers achieving things together. She has a well-developed sense of fairness — she notices and speaks up when rules aren't applied equally to everyone. He is creative in his problem-solving — he finds original routes to solutions and isn't afraid to think outside the expected approach. She expresses gratitude readily — she notices and remembers kindnesses, and thanks people without being reminded. He brings real optimism to difficult situations — when things go wrong he believes they'll improve, and that attitude is contagious. She has strong self-regulation — she can manage her emotions and impulses, and knows when to pause before reacting. He has a genuine love of learning — whatever the subject, he enjoys the process of understanding new things for its own sake. She shows natural leadership — she organises groups, makes sure everyone is included, and is bothered when someone is left out.

# PISA 2025 and Early Work Experience: The Missing Link for Turkish Students
Short Answer PISA 2025 presents two contrasting pictures for Turkey: science and reading scores are above the OECD average, but computational problem solving — the most critical skill for the future — is below the OECD average. And 53% of students skipped at least one school day in the two weeks before the test — 2.4 times the OECD average. These findings make clear that school performance alone is not enough. The missing link: real work experience. EduEntry enables students to gain international internship experience while still at school. On 8 September 2026, the OECD published PISA 2025 results, drawing on assessments of over 760,000 fifteen-year-olds across 91 countries and economies. In Turkey, 7,702 students in 203 schools participated, representing approximately 920,900 fifteen-year-olds — about 72% of that age group. The results look optimistic on the surface. Look closer, and important warnings emerge. In this article I present the PISA 2025 Turkey data as it is: what is good, what is concerning, and what needs to change. And I address a dimension the data itself cannot fully capture: the critical role of early work experience in preparing Turkish students for global competition. 
## PISA 2025 Turkey Results: The Good News First
An honest assessment starts by acknowledging real progress. Turkey is among the few countries and economies where results improved in all three subjects between 2022 and 2025 — in mathematics, reading and science. This is not a trivial achievement. Subject Turkey — Level 2+ Rate OECD Average Difference Science 81% 74% +7 points above Reading 76% 69% +7 points above Mathematics 64% 65% Near OECD average The improvement since 2015 is even more striking: the share of low-performing students (below Level 2) fell by 16 percentage points in mathematics and by 25 percentage points in science. Turkey has made genuine progress in reducing its floor. 
## The Concerning Picture: Three Critical Findings

### 1. Top-Performer Rates Remain Far Behind Global Leaders
Level 2 in PISA represents the baseline proficiency threshold. But in global competition what matters is not just crossing the threshold — it is reaching the top tier. Here is Turkey's real picture: Subject Turkey — Level 5-6 (Top Performers) OECD Avg Singapore China (B-S-J-Z) Mathematics 8% 8% 37% 54% Science 7% 7% — — Reading 4% 6% — — Turkey is at the OECD average — but the countries it needs to compete with in the global labour market are not at the OECD average; they are in the top tier. In Singapore, 1 in 3 students reaches the highest mathematics levels. In Turkey, it is 1 in 12. 
### 2. Computational Problem Solving: The AI-Era Skill — Below OECD Average
PISA 2025 measured computational problem solving for the first time — not coding, but algorithmic thinking, data interpretation and logical reasoning in digital environments. In the era when artificial intelligence is transforming the labour market, this skill is overtaking reading and mathematics in employer value. And Turkey scored below the OECD average . Why it matters: A student may have solid mathematical knowledge but still be unable to break a real problem into steps and generate an algorithmic solution. That is no longer the profile employers are looking for. PISA 2025 quantified this gap for the first time. A striking additional finding: 52% of students in Turkey use AI chatbots for schoolwork at least once a week (OECD: 46%). Tool usage is high, but computational thinking ability is low. This points to a generation that uses AI tools but has not yet developed the profile that creates value in an AI-driven world. 
### 3. The Truancy Crisis: Students Are Disconnecting From School
One of the most striking Turkey findings in PISA 2025: Indicator Turkey OECD Average Skipped at least one school day (2 weeks before test) 53% 22% Skipped at least one class 41% 24% Arrived late for school 49% 50% Agree that "school has been a waste of time" 28% 24% One in two Turkish students skipped school even during the most critical period — the two weeks before the PISA assessment. And this rate has been unchanged since 2018: 52% in 2018, 53% in 2022, 53% in 2025. This is not a random pattern — it is a structural problem. When students lose motivation, absenteeism follows. And at the root of this pattern is a school experience that has lost its connection to real life. 
## What PISA Cannot Measure: Readiness for Work
PISA is a powerful tool but a limited one: it measures academic knowledge and certain cognitive skills. It cannot measure many of the skills that determine success in working life — because those skills do not develop in a classroom. Consider: we are a country where 81% of students reach baseline science proficiency. Yet employers routinely report that new graduates "don't know how to work on real projects", "struggle with deadline management", "can't communicate effectively with clients". This contradiction is not coincidental. The gap between academic performance and workplace readiness is a structural feature of Turkey's education system — and it becomes even more visible when a student moves abroad, beginning at an international school in Dubai, the UK or elsewhere. 
## The Impact of Early Work Experience on Academic Performance
Within the PISA 2025 data, there is an illuminating finding: in Turkey, a one-unit increase in the goal-setting index is associated with a 7-point improvement in science performance — compared to an OECD average of 3 points. In other words, Turkish students who learn goal-oriented behaviour benefit from it at more than twice the OECD average rate. Work life develops exactly these behaviours: Goal-setting: Every project has a deadline; every task requires a result Self-regulation: Learning to work without waiting for a reminder Real feedback: Not "you scored 87" but "rewrite this report" — consequences are immediate and concrete Problem-solving under pressure: Problems are not clean exam questions — they are messy and ambiguous Communication: Expressing an idea in writing and speech — the skill PISA cannot measure but employers pay for Research consistently shows that students who engage with the working world early also show higher school attendance and engagement. The truancy data is worth recalling: when students cannot see why school matters, the connection breaks. A real project experience makes classroom subjects meaningful — the question "where will I use mathematics?" finds a concrete answer. 
## Closing the Computational Thinking Gap
Computational problem solving is the only area where Turkey scored below the OECD average in PISA 2025. It is also the hardest skill to teach in a classroom — because it cannot be taught without authentic context. Computational thinking involves: Decomposing a complex problem into manageable steps Pattern recognition Translating a general solution into concrete algorithms Making decisions under ambiguity and incomplete information All of these are situations encountered naturally in real work projects. A task like "categorise customer complaints and identify which product generates the most issues" is, in practice, a computational thinking exercise in a workplace setting. The Singapore gap explained: Singapore's Level 5-6 mathematics rate is 37%. This is not solely the result of excellent mathematics teaching — the Singapore education system integrates problem-solving, real-world context and early career exploration into the curriculum as inseparable elements. Turkey's system, by contrast, is oriented towards content delivery and exam preparation.

But the skills that working life requires do not appear on graduation night or on the first day at a job. They are built over years, through real experience, and they compound when started early.

Turkish students' perseverance exceeds the OECD norm. The problem is not perseverance — it is the absence of meaningful goals and experiences to channel it into.

Over 5,000 Turkish students attend international schools in Dubai. Most are in KHDA Outstanding or Very Good-rated schools — academically, they are on solid ground. ## Conclusion: Reading PISA Correctly
PISA 2025 says this about Turkey: we are progressing in baseline competency. That is real and important. But the same data also says: we lag in computational thinking, our top-performer rates are far behind global leaders, and one in two students is failing to form a genuine connection with school. The solution to this picture is not only better exam preparation. The solution is connecting students to the real world while they are still in school — giving them a concrete experience that answers "why am I learning this?". Early participation in working life creates the most natural learning environment for the skills PISA measures but the system does not sufficiently develop — goal-setting, self-regulation, computational thinking. ## How to Register for an International School in Qatar
Registering for an international school in Qatar involves four steps: completing the online application form and uploading documents, attending an assessment day (written test and parent interview), receiving an offer letter, and paying the registration fee. The process takes 3–6 weeks at most schools. Unlike Dubai, Qatar has no publicly available school quality rating system, making school research more demanding. In this guide: Qatar education system · oversight structure · curriculum types · popular schools and areas · fees · step-by-step application · how Qatar compares to Dubai · tips for expat families 
## Qatar's Education System: Overview
Private international schools in Qatar operate under the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MOEHE). As of 2024, Doha has approximately 170 private schools. The vast majority of the student population — unlike Qatari nationals — comes from expat families. Compared to Dubai's KHDA system, there is one significant difference: Qatar does not publish a standardised, publicly accessible quality rating for schools. MOEHE conducts inspections and publishes reports, but these are not as easily accessible as KHDA reports. This makes school selection harder; personal referrals and on-site visits become more important. For expat families: expats in Qatar are concentrated in construction, energy (QatarEnergy), healthcare and education. The expat community grew significantly following the 2022 FIFA World Cup infrastructure boom. 
## Curriculum Types: Which School Fits Your Family?

### Curriculum Options in Doha
British (IGCSE / A-Level) Most common curriculum. Doha College, Cambridge International, Park House. Structurally closest to the Turkish system for transition. IB (International Baccalaureate) Qatar Academy (Qatar Foundation), ISL Qatar. High academic standards, strong university preparation. Fees at the upper band. American (AP / Common Core) American School of Doha (ASD). Ideal for families targeting US universities. Long waiting list. Indian Curriculum (CBSE / ICSE) DPS Modern Indian School, MES. Serves the largest expat community in Qatar. Most affordable option. 
## Qatar's Leading International Schools

### Doha College
Operating since the 1980s, Doha College is one of Qatar's most established international schools, following the British curriculum (IGCSE and A-Level). Located in Al Messila. Annual fees in the QAR 45,000–65,000 range. 
### American School of Doha (ASD)
Founded in 1950, ASD follows the American curriculum and has a strong track record for US university admissions. Demand is high; waiting lists can be long, especially at secondary level. Fees QAR 55,000–75,000. 
### Qatar Academy (Education City)
Qatar Academy is part of Qatar Foundation and offers the IB curriculum on the Education City campus. Qatari nationals have priority in admissions, making competition for expat places higher. Fees QAR 40,000–70,000. 
### ISL Qatar
ISL Qatar offers both IB and British curricula and stands out for small class sizes and strong EAL support — a good option for children whose English is still developing.

## Robert Kolej Fee 2026-27: The Number
Robert Kolej's annual tuition: 2,488,200 TL — covering tuition only. Boarding, transport and meals add an estimated 500,000–700,000 TL annually for some students. Founded in 1863, it follows its own rigorous curriculum and awards a Turkish national diploma — Turkey's most selective school by admission criteria. The price reflects real academic value. ## What Does the Same Budget Buy in Dubai?
At 1 AED = 13.65 TL, Dubai's KHDA Outstanding IB school Dubai International Academy (DIA) costs approximately 1,012,000–1,202,000 TL annually — less than half of Robert Kolej. ## The Real Cost Gap
Fee tables alone are misleading. Turkey's TL-based fees face 40-70% annual inflation increases, require pre-school exam prep costs, and are paid from taxed income. Dubai's AED-based fees are inflation-shielded, KHDA-regulated, and paid from zero-income-tax salaries. The five-year total cost differential is far larger than the single-year comparison suggests. There is also an opportunity cost to consider. A family paying 2.5 million TL annually in Turkey is simultaneously not building AED savings, not benefiting from Dubai's zero capital gains, and not accessing the salary multiples that most Turkish professionals report after relocating to the Gulf. Over a five-year secondary school period, these combined effects regularly account for more than the school fee gap itself. 
## Admissions: Entrance Exam vs Open Enrolment
One factor the fee table doesn't capture: access. Robert Kolej admits students through one of Turkey's most competitive entrance processes. Preparation typically begins years in advance, adds significant tuition and prep costs, and creates considerable pressure for the whole family. Dubai's KHDA Outstanding schools — DIA, GEMS World Academy, Dubai American Academy — admit students based on academic records and an interview, with no entrance exam. For a family relocating to Dubai, this is not a minor administrative detail. 
## Five-Year Total Cost: TL vs AED
A single year's comparison understates the real picture. Robert Kolej's fees have increased by an average of 55% annually over the past three years. At a conservative 45% annual increase, a family paying 2,488,200 TL today will pay approximately 13.5 million TL in year five — equivalent at today's exchange rate to around $370,000 for five years. DIA in Dubai, with KHDA fee caps limiting annual increases to single-digit percentages, projects to approximately $120,000–$140,000 over the same period. This calculation excludes additional Turkey costs (transport, meals, boarding for some, entrance-exam prep) and excludes Dubai's zero income tax — a structural salary advantage that Turkish families in the UAE consistently report as the decisive factor in the overall financial equation. 
## Curriculum Outcome: Turkish Diploma vs IB Diploma
Robert Kolej graduates receive a Turkish national diploma — highly respected within Turkey, but not internationally recognised as a standalone university entrance qualification. Turkish families applying to US, UK or European universities typically need supplementary qualifications: SAT, A-levels or AP courses. Koç Okulu and ENKA, by contrast, award the IB Diploma — recognised by over 5,000 universities worldwide including Oxford, MIT and Sciences Po, with no additional testing needed. Dubai IB schools offer the same international passport. For a family with global university ambitions, this is a structural consideration that sits above the fee comparison. 
## Who Should Consider Robert Kolej — and Who Shouldn't
Robert Kolej remains one of the genuinely great schools in Turkey. For families committed to remaining in Istanbul, it represents exceptional academic rigour and a powerful domestic network. For families considering international relocation or global university pathways, the fee-to-outcome ratio versus Dubai IB schools requires honest evaluation. The question isn't just "Can we afford Robert Kolej?" — it's "Does Robert Kolej serve the future we're building?"

# School Enrolment in Canada: Step-by-Step Guide for Turkish Families
Ozlem Cimen — Note from the coach My close familiarity with Canada came through working with a family who relocated there. When I returned, I realised just how good Canadian public schools actually are — and how much smoother the transition is for families who understand the system in advance. This guide is my attempt to show you the surprises before they arrive. Canada's key advantage: All public schools are high-quality and completely free once you meet the residency requirement. Private school costs are significantly lower than in other destination countries. A genuinely multicultural environment means families integrate faster than almost anywhere else. 
## Canada's Three Main School Systems
Canada is a federal country, so each province runs its own education system with its own school boards. The provinces most popular with expat families are Ontario, British Columbia (BC) and — to a lesser extent — Quebec. 🇨🇦 Ontario (GTA) TDSB & Peel Board Highest concentration of expat families. Elementary (K–6), Middle (7–8), High (9–12). Both English and French immersion streams available. 🇨🇦 British Columbia (Vancouver) VSD & VSB More flexible curriculum. Large international family population due to Pacific location. Nature-centred education options. 🇨🇦 Quebec (Montreal) French-dominant School system is largely in French. Limited English options. Strongest language barrier of any major Canadian province. 🆓 Public School Completely Free Open to all qualifying families. Free with a work or study permit. Very high quality; ESL support available in most schools. 
## Public School vs Private School
Factor Public School Private School Cost Completely free CAD $8,000–$20,000+ / year Curriculum Provincial standard IB, Cambridge, Montessori Class size 25–35 students 15–25 students Application Online, straightforward Interview + assessment test Language support ESL programme available Limited or none Entrance exam None Usually required 
## Enrolment Process: 7 Steps
1 Obtain Proof of Residency — A lease agreement or utility bill (electricity, water). This is mandatory for school registration. 2 Apply for a SIN (Social Insurance Number) — Required before school registration can be completed. 3 Get your birth certificate translated — A notarised English translation of the original Turkish document is required. 4 Verify vaccination records — Turkish vaccination records are generally recognised, but may require a notarised English translation. 5 Register with the local school board — Log in to the TDSB, Peel or VSB online portal and complete the application. 6 Academic placement assessment — The school assigns a grade level based on age and an academic assessment. 7 Attend orientation — Most schools offer an orientation session in late August. Highly recommended for families new to the Canadian system. 
## Language Barrier and ESL Support
One of the strongest advantages of Canadian public schools is the ESL (English as a Second Language) and EAL (English as an Additional Language) programme built into most schools. Quebec is the exception — French immersion is the default there, creating a much heavier language burden than Ontario or BC. Practical tip: Begin intensive English preparation with your child before the move. Language adaptation becomes significantly harder after age 14. Online language courses during the summer months can make a meaningful difference to the first year of school. 
## Application Timeline
June–July: Prepare proof of residency documentation August: SIN application, birth certificate translation, vaccination record check September (immediately on arrival): Register via TDSB / Peel / VSB portal September (first week): School orientation — compulsory or strongly recommended 
## Which City Is Right for Your Family?
The city you choose in Canada directly shapes your school options. Each major city has distinct advantages and constraints for expat families. Toronto (GTA — including Mississauga and Brampton): Home to Canada's largest expat community. The richest options for Islamic schools, Turkish supermarkets, mosques and social networks. Strong school boards include TDSB and Peel District. The trade-off: Toronto has the highest cost of living in Canada, particularly for rent. Vancouver (BC): A smaller but tight-knit expat community. Nature-focused lifestyle and mild climate attract many families. BC's curriculum is slightly more flexible than Ontario's, and French Immersion options are strong. International families are well-represented, so children adapt quickly. Montreal (Quebec): The lowest cost of living, but the highest language barrier. The public school system is largely in French; English-medium options are limited. If English-language education is the priority, Montreal deserves careful consideration before committing. Choosing your city — four factors to weigh: Your child's age and English level; your family's social needs (expat community, mosque, Turkish grocery); your rent and cost-of-living tolerance; your employer's location. When these four are evaluated together, the right city usually becomes clear quickly. Author Ozlem Cimen International education consultant and founder of Edualist. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can foreign students attend Canadian public schools for free?
Families with Permanent Residency (PR) or certain visa types can access public schools at no cost. Children arriving on a student visa typically pay CAD $10,000–$14,000 per year in school fees. 
### What is the most important difference between Ontario and BC school systems?
Ontario operates a 12-year system leading to the OSSD (Ontario Secondary School Diploma). BC has a similar structure but places stronger emphasis on French Immersion options. Both provinces have strong IB-authorised schools. 
### What documents are needed for school registration in Canada?
Passport or birth certificate, proof of address, vaccination records, and a notarised English translation of your child's previous school transcript. 
### When does the Canadian school year start?
The school year typically begins in the first week of September and ends in late June. Some schools use a trimester system. A January mid-year entry is available at some schools. 
### Which Canadian city is best for expat families?
Toronto (including Mississauga and Brampton) hosts Canada's largest expat community — strongest for Islamic schools, Turkish groceries and social networks. Vancouver offers a smaller but cohesive expat community alongside a nature-focused lifestyle that appeals to many families.

Back to Blog Summary A guide to school enrollment in France for expat families — covering the centralized national curriculum, administrative steps, language considerations, and the choice between French public schools and international options. France runs its education system centrally — the Ministry of National Education (Ministère de l'Éducation Nationale) sets the same curriculum nationwide. That's good news: wherever in France you live, the curriculum is the same, making school transfers straightforward. The harder parts are the French language barrier and the bureaucratic process — both of which this guide addresses directly. Ozlem Cimen — Note from the coach When I work with families relocating to France, I notice the same pattern: students take longer to adapt to the French system than expected. The language barrier is harder than anticipated; the bureaucracy slower. I wrote this guide so families see the reality first — not the romanticised version. Personal note: Ozlem Cimen raised her own children in Lycée Français International de Rangoun (Yangon), Lycée français de Bakou, Lycée Français Pierre Loti d'Istanbul and Lycée Français Jean Mermoz de Dubai. ## The French School System: Structure and Stages
Ages 3–11 
#### École Maternelle & Primaire
Nursery (maternelle) from age 3; primary school (primaire) from age 6. State schools are free. Compulsory education begins at 6. Ages 11–15 
#### Collège
4-year middle school. Same curriculum for all students. Ends with the Brevet exam. Foreign language choice during this period is significant. Ages 15–18 
#### Lycée & Baccalauréat
3-year high school. General (Général), Technological or Vocational Bac options. The Baccalauréat is the gateway to French university entry. All ages 
#### Lycée Français & International
500+ Lycées Français worldwide. Lycées Internationaux de Paris offer IB and international sections. The global network is a major advantage for mobile families. Key advantage: France's Lycée Français network spans 500+ schools worldwide. A child who starts in a Lycée Français in France can transfer to any school in the network globally with minimal disruption — a significant advantage for frequently relocating families. 
## Class System: Counting Down
French class numbering runs in reverse — which surprises most non-French families. The higher the number in the name, the younger the year group: 
#### French Year Group System
6ème (Sixième) Collège Year 1 — ages 11–12 5ème (Cinquième) Collège Year 2 — ages 12–13 4ème (Quatrième) Collège Year 3 — ages 13–14 3ème (Troisième) Collège final year + Brevet exam 2nde (Seconde) Lycée Year 1 — ages 15–16 1ère (Première) Lycée Year 2 — ages 16–17 Terminale Lycée final year + Baccalauréat 
## French Language Preparation
French state schools teach in French. For students with a language barrier, specialised language support programmes called UPE2A (Unité Pédagogique pour Élèves Allophones Arrivants) are available. These programmes are designed to accelerate newly arrived students' adaptation to French — they are a support mechanism, not a penalty. Warning: French is harder to learn quickly than many families expect — particularly compared to English. For children over 14, starting a French state school without any French is very difficult. I recommend reaching at least A2 level before enrolment. 
## Enrolment Process: 7 Steps
1 Register at the Mairie (town hall) — After arriving in France, submit your residence declaration at the local town hall. This document is required for school enrolment. 2 Identify your catchment school — In France, children must attend the school assigned to their residential address (carte scolaire). Switching sectors is possible under specific conditions. 3 Apply at the Mairie or school — For primary, apply at the town hall. For middle and high school, apply directly to the school (Rectorat/DSDEN). 4 UPE2A language assessment — If French is insufficient, your child will be directed to the UPE2A class first. This is designed to support, not delay. 5 Year group placement — The school assigns a year group based on age and academic level. Children without French may be placed one year back — this is standard practice. 6 Submit documents — Deliver required documents to the school administration. Use an accredited translator for documents requiring translation. 7 Start intensive French — Begin Alliance Française or private lessons before the school start date. Early language preparation is the single most decisive factor in a smooth first year.

## [School Enrolment in Germany: Gymnasium & Documents](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/school-enrolment-germany/)

Back to Blog Summary A step-by-step guide to school enrollment in Germany for expat families. Covers the federal education system's state-by-state variations, school types, mandatory registration, and key practical tips. Germany's federal structure means each of its 16 states (Bundesländer) runs its own school system under its own laws — which makes the system look complex at first glance. But once you understand the structure, it becomes manageable — and for the right family, genuinely advantageous. This guide walks through the school types, the enrolment process, and the practical realities expat families face in Germany. Ozlem Cimen — Note from the coach Every time I work with a family moving to Germany, I see the same moment: Gymnasium, Realschule, Gesamtschule — and on top of that, different in every state. I had that confusion too when I first studied the system. I wrote this guide to clear it away and give you a clear starting point. Important: The academic year in Germany varies by state — it starts in August or September depending on the Bundesland. The Anmeldung (address registration) is mandatory and must be completed before school enrolment — do this first. 
## The German School System: A Multi-Tier Structure
Primary school (Grundschule) in Germany runs for 4 years (6 years in Berlin and Brandenburg). After primary school, children are directed into different school types based on academic performance. This transition is a critical decision point — families need to be prepared for it. University Track 
#### Gymnasium
The highest academic path. Leads to the Abitur exam, which gives direct university entry. Years 5–12/13. High academic expectations throughout. Prerequisite: strong German language proficiency. Practical Track 
#### Realschule
Mid-level academic programme. Opens pathways to vocational training or transfer to Gymnasium. Years 5–10. More flexible, a good option for children still building German. Comprehensive 
#### Gesamtschule
All-in-one comprehensive school that streams students internally as they progress. Flexibility makes it a good starting point for expat families — especially those still building German language skills. English-Medium 
#### International School
IB, American or British curriculum. No German required. Common in Berlin, Munich, Hamburg and Frankfurt. Annual fees €10,000–€30,000. Critical warning: Starting a German state school with no German language ability is very difficult. Rushed enrolments without language preparation create stress for both the child and the family. Assess language level first — then choose the school type. 
## The Critical Issue: German Language Level
German state schools teach in German. Your child's language level directly determines which school type makes sense. The table below is a starting guide: German level CEFR Recommendation No German A0 International school or intensive German course + Vorbereitungsklasse Basic German A1–A2 Gesamtschule with Förderklasse (support class) Intermediate German B1–B2 Realschule or Gesamtschule; academic tutoring recommended Advanced German C1+ Ready for any school type including Gymnasium 
### What is a Vorbereitungsklasse?
Many German state schools offer a Vorbereitungsklasse (preparatory class) for newly arrived children with limited German. These classes provide intensive German language instruction and prepare children for integration into the mainstream school. They typically last one year and are free in state schools. 
### Let's find the right school type for your child's situation
Clarifying your school strategy before you move saves significant time and stress. Book a Free Session 
## Differences by State and City
Each of Germany's 16 states has its own education laws. For expat families, the most commonly chosen cities break down as follows: Berlin — Gesamtschule-dominated, the widest international school network. Most accommodating to expat families. Primary school runs 6 years here. Munich (Bavaria) — Germany's most selective state for schools. High Gymnasium standards. Ideal if your child has a strong academic profile and solid German. Hamburg — Flexible structure, strong international school options. Cosmopolitan port city culture. Frankfurt — Major expat hub due to financial sector; large international school network. A natural first choice for finance-sector families. 
## Enrolment Process: 8 Steps
1 Complete the Anmeldung (address registration) — Within 14 days of arriving in Germany, you must register your address at the local Bürgeramt. This document is required for school enrolment. 2 Assess your child's German level — Choose the school type based on language ability. If needed, start an intensive German course first — do not rush this step. 3 Identify your local school — In most German states, state schools are assigned by residential catchment area (Schulbezirk). Contact the local Schulamt to find out which school you are zoned for. 4 Visit the school and meet the principal — German schools usually require an appointment for new pupil admissions. Contact the school in advance; bring a translator if possible. 5 Academic placement assessment — The school may conduct a short assessment to determine the right year group. This is standard practice, particularly for German and maths. 6 Prepare the required documents — Anmeldungsbestätigung, passport, previous school transcripts (German or English translation), vaccination record. Some states may request additional documents. 7 Complete the enrolment form — For state schools, register via the Schulamt or directly with the school administration. For international schools, apply directly to the school. 8 Plan for integration and language support — The first months are intensive for both child and family. Vorbereitungsklasse, private German lessons and social activities all accelerate settling in.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is there a Turkish school in Germany?
Not a full-time MEB-curriculum Turkish state school. Germany has around 4 million people of Turkish origin, and expat community associations in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Hamburg run weekend Turkish language schools. These help children maintain Turkish literacy. For full-time education, expat families in Germany enrol children in state schools (Gymnasium, Gesamtschule) or international schools. See our guide to Turkish schools in Germany → 
### My child speaks no German — what should I do?
Start intensive German lessons immediately. Then choose a Gesamtschule with a Vorbereitungsklasse programme, or start at an international school. Rushing into a state school without language preparation typically backfires. 
### Are Turkish school grades recognised in Germany?
Yes — Turkish education documents are recognised. Transcripts should be translated into German; some states require an apostille stamp. Class placement is reassessed by the school. 
### Can my child start directly at a Gymnasium?
If your child has a strong academic level and solid German, yes. Without German proficiency, Gymnasium is very challenging — starting at Gesamtschule is generally the healthier choice and does not close the Gymnasium path later. 
### Which city is easiest for integration?
Berlin, with its multicultural character and wide international school network, is the most flexible city. Munich is academically strong but requires a more integrated German-language environment. For expat community connections, Cologne and the Rhine-Ruhr area have the highest concentration of international families in Germany.

Back to Blog Summary A guide for expat families enrolling their children in Italian schools — covering the tiered school system, mandatory education requirements, key registration steps, and international school options in major cities. Italy is as renowned for its historic education tradition as for its culture and art. For expat families moving to Milan, Rome, Florence or elsewhere in Italy, the school system looks very different at first. This guide walks through Italy's school structure, the enrolment process, and the practical details step by step. ## The Italian School System: Stages by Age
Compulsory education in Italy covers ages 6–16. The system is divided into three main stages, each with its own school types. Ages 6–11 
#### Scuola Primaria
5-year primary school. State schools are free. Foreign children can enrol directly; language support availability varies by school. Ages 11–14 
#### Scuola Secondaria I
3-year middle school. Same curriculum for all students. Ends with the Licenza Media exam, which influences high school choice. Ages 14–19 
#### Liceo / Istituto Tecnico
High school level. Specialisations include Liceo Scientifico (sciences), Classico (humanities/Latin/Greek) and Linguistico (languages). Ends with the Maturità exam for university entry. All ages 
#### International School
IB, British or American curriculum. Common in Milan and Rome. English-medium instruction. Annual fees approximately €10,000–€25,000. 
## Italian Language Preparation
Italian state schools teach in Italian. However, the Italian school system tends to be welcoming to foreign students. Most state schools offer a laboratorio linguistico (language support programme) for students with limited Italian. Good news: Italian is relatively straightforward to learn for children — particularly compared to German or French. Children aged 6–12 tend to adapt remarkably quickly. With patience through the first 3–6 months, integration is typically very successful. 
## Enrolment Process: 7 Steps
1 Obtain a Codice Fiscale — Italy's tax identification number is required for all official processes. It can be obtained from an Agenzia delle Entrate office or the Italian consulate before arrival. 2 Register your address (Residenza) — Submit a residence declaration at the local town hall (Comune). This step is mandatory before school enrolment. 3 Research local school options — Italian state schools are assigned by residential area. The local school administration office (Ufficio Scolastico) can tell you which school you are zoned for. 4 Pre-register January–February — Enrolment for the following academic year typically opens in January. Applications are made through the MIUR online portal. 5 Academic placement assessment — The school will conduct a short assessment to determine the appropriate year group, testing Italian language and maths level. 6 Submit documents — Deliver the required documents in person to the school administration. Use an accredited translator for documents requiring Italian translation. 7 Plan language support and integration — Enrol in the laboratorio linguistico programme. Private Italian lessons (ripetizioni) also accelerate adaptation significantly.

## Milan or Rome?
Milan — Italy's business capital, with the widest international school network. Higher cost of living, but strong educational quality and a large expat community. Rome — A richer cultural and historical environment. State schools are generally strong, and the cost of living is slightly lower than Milan. A good balance of quality and affordability. Practical tip: Private tutoring (ripetizioni) is a deeply embedded part of Italian culture. Finding a private Italian tutor for your child is easy and affordable. Two to three hours per week in the first term makes a very noticeable difference to adaptation speed. 
## Italy's Education System in International Context
Italy's 2022 PISA results placed it above the OECD average in reading (482 vs 476) and close to average in mathematics (471 vs 472). These aggregate figures mask significant regional variation: schools in northern Italy (Lombardy, Trentino, Veneto) consistently outperform those in southern regions by margins of 30–50 PISA points — a gap broadly comparable to one full school year of learning. For families settling in Milan, Bologna or Turin, this regional advantage is an important contextual factor. The Liceo Classico track — Italy's most academically prestigious secondary route, centred on Latin, ancient Greek, philosophy and literature — produces graduates with unusually strong analytical writing and critical reasoning skills. Research by the Italian National Institute for the Evaluation of the Educational System (INVALSI) shows that Liceo Classico graduates achieve the highest average university graduation rates of any Italian secondary track. 
## Language Integration: What the Research Shows
Research on child second language acquisition consistently shows that children aged 6–12 achieve near-native fluency in a new language within 2–3 years of full immersion, provided social integration is supported. The Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) defines B1 (independent user) as achievable within approximately 200 hours of instruction for a motivated young learner. With Italian-language schooling and active social participation, most expat children reach B1 within the first academic year. This timeline is considerably faster than adult language acquisition, which averages 400–600 hours for the same level. The implication: prioritising enrolment in an Italian state school — rather than defaulting to an international school for language comfort — is often the better long-term choice for children who will remain in Italy for more than two years. State schools are free — only small administrative contributions and materials costs apply (approximately €100–€300/year).

Yes — Turkish education documents are recognised in Italy. They must be submitted with an apostille stamp and an accredited Italian translation. 
### When is the Liceo choice made?
At the end of middle school, at age 14. This is a significant decision — your child's interests, language level and long-term goals should all be weighed together carefully.

## [School Enrolment in the Netherlands: Family Guide](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/school-enrolment-netherlands/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/school-enrolment-netherlands/  
**Date:** 2026-06-07

Back to Blog Summary A practical guide for families relocating to the Netherlands — covering the Dutch primary school system, the CITO transition test, ISK language bridge programme, enrolment steps, documents checklist, and international school options in Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Eindhoven with 2025-26 fee ranges. The Netherlands is one of Europe's most expat-friendly countries for education — over 90% of the Dutch population speaks fluent English, and a wide network of international schools operates across all major cities. This guide walks through the Dutch school structure and the enrolment process step by step. The Netherlands' key advantage: Many state schools offer a bilingual (TTO — Tweetalig Onderwijs) stream where half the lessons are in English. This significantly reduces the language barrier and eases your child's transition. 
## The Dutch School System: Three Pathways
Dutch primary school (Basisschool) runs for 8 years, from age 4 to 12. The CITO test in the final year determines which secondary school track your child enters. This transition is critical — families should plan for it well in advance. University Track 
#### VWO
6-year programme, the highest academic track. Direct entry to research universities (WO). Gymnasium VWO also teaches Latin and Ancient Greek. High academic expectations throughout. Applied University Track 
#### HAVO
5-year programme. Leads to applied universities (HBO). Slightly more flexible than VWO. Ideal for upper-mid academic ability. A good stepping stone — HAVO graduates can transfer to VWO with strong grades. Vocational Track 
#### VMBO
4-year programme leading to vocational education (MBO). Practical and applied focus. Dutch vocational education is highly regarded and well-connected to the labour market. Expat Families 
#### International School
IB, British or American curriculum. No Dutch required. Strong options in Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Eindhoven. Annual fees approximately €11,000–€24,000. 
## The CITO Test: The Critical Moment
In the final year of primary school (groep 8, age 12), the CITO test determines which secondary school track a child is recommended for. For children who are still developing their Dutch, this test can be a significant source of stress — and an unfair disadvantage. Practical advice: If you are relocating to the Netherlands less than one year before the CITO test, I recommend either starting at an international school or exploring options to defer the test. Your child should not enter this system at a structural disadvantage because of a recent move. 
## Dutch vs English: Language of Instruction
The Netherlands is one of Europe's most accommodating countries for English-speaking families. Many state schools offer TTO bilingual streams — half the curriculum delivered in English. International schools operate entirely in English and follow IB, British or American programmes. 💡 
#### ISK — International Transition Class
ISK (Internationale Schakelklas) is a 1–2 year bridge programme for newly arrived foreign students. It builds Dutch language skills and prepares children to enter the mainstream school system. Available in most major cities. 
## The ISK Programme: A Language Bridge for Newly Arrived Students
ISK (Internationale Schakelklas — International Transition Class) is a free, state-funded bridge programme for foreign students who do not yet speak Dutch. It is available in virtually every major Dutch city — Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam, Eindhoven and Utrecht all have multiple ISK providers. 
### How ISK Works
The programme typically runs for one year, though strong learners can complete it in 6–8 months. Alongside intensive Dutch language instruction, ISK covers core maths, science and social studies. Teachers generally use English as a support language — a practical advantage that expat families consistently highlight. ISK also functions as an assessment period: at the end of the programme, teachers recommend whether the child should enter VMBO, HAVO or VWO. Academic performance in maths and science is especially influential in this recommendation. Children from Turkey often arrive ahead of their Dutch peers in these subjects — a confidence anchor during the language transition. One question to ask every ISK school: "What percentage of your ISK graduates are placed in HAVO or VWO?" The answer tells you more about programme quality than any brochure. 
## Enrolment Process: 7 Steps
1 Obtain your BSN (Burgerservicenummer) — A Citizen Service Number is required for all official processes in the Netherlands, including school enrolment. Register at your local municipality (Gemeente) to receive it. 2 Register at the Gemeente — By law, you must register your address at the local municipality within 5 days of arriving (inschrijving). School enrolment cannot be completed without this. 3 Decide on school type — International school, bilingual TTO stream, or ISK programme? Your child's age, Dutch language level and academic profile determine the right path. 4 Apply directly to the school — There is no centralised admissions system in the Netherlands. Each school is contacted separately. Popular international schools in The Hague and Amsterdam have waiting lists of 1–2 years. 5 Attend a placement assessment — The school evaluates academic level and language ability. Any CITO results, school reports or standardised test scores you can provide will be used. 6 Submit your documents — See the documents table below. Translations of foreign-language documents must be prepared in advance. 7 Plan language support — Even at international schools, building Dutch alongside English pays long-term dividends. ISK, private tutoring or community language classes all help. 
## Required Documents
Document Notes BSN certificate Citizen Service Number — mandatory Inschrijvingsbewijs Gemeente address registration certificate Verblijfsvergunning Residence permit or visa School reports Last 2 years — translated to English or Dutch by a sworn translator Vaccination record Vaccinatiebewijs CITO result If available — used to recommend secondary track 
## Which City?
Amsterdam — The Netherlands' most cosmopolitan city. High cost of living and competitive housing. English-medium international schools: Amsterdam International Community School (AICS) , British School of Amsterdam and Amity International School Amsterdam . Annual fees €14,000–€22,000. The Hague (Den Haag) — Home to international organisations and diplomatic missions; the most popular city for diplomatic and tech expat families. International School of The Hague (ISH) , with students from 70+ countries, is one of the most established international schools in the Netherlands. American School of The Hague offers a US curriculum. Annual fees €17,000–€24,000. Waiting lists apply at several schools. Rotterdam — Modern, multicultural, and more affordable than Amsterdam. International School Rotterdam (IRIS) offers full English instruction at secondary level; Rotterdam International Secondary School (RISS) is another well-regarded option. Annual fees €12,000–€18,000. Eindhoven — Popular with employees of ASML, Philips and other tech companies. International School Eindhoven (ISE) blends IB and British curriculum in a small-class, family-friendly environment. Annual fees €11,000–€17,000. 
## International English Schools in the Netherlands: City and Cost
Dutch state schools are free (small materials contributions expected). International schools offer English-medium instruction and are the choice of most expat families. The Hague and Amsterdam schools often have waiting lists due to high demand — apply at least 12 months before your target start date. If you're also considering Canada as a destination, see our Canada school registration guide → 
## The Turkish Community in the Netherlands
The Netherlands is home to approximately 400,000–450,000 people of Turkish origin — one of the largest Turkish diaspora communities in Europe. The community dates back to the guest-worker programmes of the 1960s and has since grown into a well-established third- and fourth-generation presence. For newly relocating expat families, this existing network is a genuine practical resource. 
### Where Turkish Families Settle
Rotterdam (~80,000–100,000) has the largest expat community in the Netherlands, concentrated in the Feijenoord, Delfshaven and Charlois districts. Multilingual doctors, pharmacists, lawyers and private tutors are easier to find here than anywhere else in the country — a significant practical advantage during the settling-in period. Amsterdam (~70,000–80,000) — Slotervaart, Nieuw-West and Osdorp. Higher cost of living than Rotterdam, but more diverse job market and the widest range of international schools. The Hague (~30,000–40,000) — More compact community, but the presence of the Turkish Embassy provides convenient access to consular and official document services — useful when processing school paperwork. Eindhoven and Utrecht are growing in popularity, particularly among Turkish engineers and researchers employed at ASML, Philips, NXP and the university hospitals. 
### Turkish Language Options for Children
There is no state-funded Turkish school in the Netherlands (the OALT mother-tongue programme was largely phased out in the 2000s). However, expat community associations in Rotterdam and Amsterdam run Saturday Turkish language and culture classes. Online Turkish tutors — typically 2–3 sessions per week — have become the most practical option for maintaining literacy in Turkish while children attend school in English or Dutch. 
## Bringing Turkish School Documents to the Netherlands
School documents issued in Turkey require official authentication before they are accepted by Dutch schools and the DUO (Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs — the Dutch education authority). The process has four stages: Collect school documents: Last 2 years of report cards, student transfer certificate (school stamp + principal signature), vaccination record, passport copy. Apostille: District Ministry of Education (İlçe MEB) approval, then Apostille stamp from the Governor's Office (Kaymakamlık/Valilik) — free of charge, 1–5 working days. Sworn English translation: Use a certified sworn translator and notarise. English translation is the most practical choice — sworn Dutch translators are hard to find in Turkey. DUO recognition: For secondary diplomas or if requested by the school, submit to DUO via duo.nl for foreign qualification recognition. Timing: The apostille and translation process in Turkey takes 2–3 weeks on average. Start at least 6 weeks before your planned enrolment date.
