### Do we need to learn Dutch?
For day-to-day life, English is sufficient in most Dutch cities. For children integrating into the Dutch school system long-term, Dutch language acquisition is important for social and academic progress. For short-stay expat families, international schools remove this requirement entirely. 
### Is the IB Diploma recognised by Dutch universities?
Yes — IB Diploma is fully recognised by Dutch universities. Some programmes have numerus fixus (entry caps) with minimum score requirements. For competitive programmes such as Medicine at UvA or TU Delft engineering, check specific admission thresholds in advance. 
### How long are international school waiting lists?
At popular schools in The Hague and Amsterdam, waiting lists can run 1–2 years for sought-after year groups. Apply as early as possible — ideally before you have a confirmed relocation date. 
### International school or Dutch state school?
For short-term relocations (under 3 years), international schools provide a smoother transition. For long-term stays where Dutch language integration matters, a Dutch state school — particularly one with a TTO bilingual stream — offers better language development and future opportunities in the Netherlands. 
### What is the ISK programme and does my child qualify?
ISK (Internationale Schakelklas) is a free 1–2 year Dutch language bridge programme for newly arrived foreign students aged 6–18 who do not yet speak Dutch. It is available in all major Dutch cities. After ISK, students are assessed and placed into VMBO, HAVO or VWO. Strong maths and science skills — common among children from Turkey — carry significant weight in that placement decision. 
### Are Turkish school documents accepted in the Netherlands?
Yes — apostille-stamped and officially translated (English or Dutch) school documents from Turkey are accepted by Dutch schools and the DUO education authority. The process: District MEB approval → Apostille at the Governor's Office (free) → sworn translator + notary → submit to school or DUO. Allow 2–3 weeks in Turkey before your move. 
### Rotterdam or Amsterdam — which is better for expat families?
Rotterdam has the largest expat community (~80,000–100,000) and the lowest cost of living among major Dutch cities; finding multilingual tutors, doctors and legal advisors is easiest there. Amsterdam offers more diverse employment and a wider range of international schools. Eindhoven is the best value option for tech-sector families, with quality international schooling at lower fees. 
### What school start age applies in the Netherlands?
Children may start primary school (Basisschool) at age 4; attendance becomes compulsory at 5. This is 1–2 years earlier than Turkey, and early entry has meaningful social integration benefits — particularly for children who are not yet fluent in Dutch or English.

## [Should I Send My Child to School Abroad?](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/should-my-child-study-abroad/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/should-my-child-study-abroad/  
**Date:** 2026-06-07

Back to Blog Summary A practical framework to help expat families decide whether to pursue international education abroad — moving beyond the romanticized view to address real benefits, challenges, and the right questions to ask. I've heard this question from hundreds of expat families over the years — in WhatsApp groups, over coffee in Dubai, from mothers calling from Singapore, from fathers who just moved to London. And every time I say the same thing: there is no right or wrong answer to "should I send my child abroad?" But there are good questions to ask. According to TÜİK, more than 5.5 million Turkish citizens now live outside Turkey — and recent migration data show the fastest-growing segment is skilled professionals aged 25–44. International schooling is no longer a niche choice; it is an everyday reality for millions of expat families. This guide cuts through the romanticism and gets to the truth. Note from Ozlem Cimen I made this decision myself. When we moved abroad with young children, there were tears — including mine. But today, watching my children grow up across different countries and cultures, I would make that decision again every time. One thing I've learned from my own experience and hundreds of coaching sessions: the families who navigate this best are the ones who ask the hardest questions of themselves before they pack a suitcase. Before you read on: This decision is not only about education quality. Your child's personality, your family's financial resources, your motivation for moving and your long-term plans are equally decisive factors. 
## What International Schooling Really Gives You — and the Honest Challenges
Search "international school advantages" and you'll find glossy success stories. Here is the unvarnished version. 
### What it genuinely delivers
Multilingual fluency — the most concrete gain. Research consistently shows children exposed to a second language early develop measurable advantages in cognitive flexibility, problem-solving and multi-perspective thinking. Global university access — IB Diploma and A-Level open doors not just in the UK or US but at leading universities worldwide. Cultural intelligence, global network, adaptability — these don't show up on a CV; they show up in character. 
### What is genuinely hard
Language barrier and adjustment period — typically 6–18 months of pressure on both academic and social fronts. Social network disruption and loneliness risk — especially significant for children who move during adolescence. High financial burden — school fees, cost of living, language courses and preparation costs must all be factored together. Identity complexity — "not fully from there, not fully from here" is one of the most frequently cited experiences of expat children raised abroad. Equivalency challenges on return — if the family eventually moves back to Turkey, foreign qualifications require a formal recognition process. 
#### ✦ Strengths
Multilingual fluency and global mindset Strong school profile via IB or A-Level Cultural intelligence and adaptability Global friendships and professional network Independence and self-confidence Access to world universities Critical-thinking-focused education 
#### ◆ Real Challenges
Language barrier (6–18 months) Social network disruption and loneliness High cost — school + living expenses Identity complexity: "between two worlds" Equivalency issues if returning to Turkey Increased parental stress Distance from extended family and support network 
## The Age Factor: When Is the Right Time?
The single most common question I receive: "when should we start?" The answer is both neurobiological and practical — age shapes both language adaptation and social-emotional adjustment. Age group Language adaptation Social adjustment Academic risk Overall 3–6 Very easy Easy Very low Ideal window 6–10 Easy Easy Low Highly suitable 10–13 Moderate Moderate Moderate Suitable with planning 13–15 Harder Difficult Moderate–High Intensive preparation needed 15–18 Difficult Difficult High Strong support essential The neuroscience: Research shows children up to age 10 can acquire a second language to near-native level and without an accent. After that, language learning is still entirely possible — but it demands significantly more effort, time and emotional resilience. This table is not a verdict; I've seen teenagers move at 16 and thrive. But a 16-year-old transition requires a fundamentally different and more intensive support system than a move at age 7. 
## Will Turkish Be Lost? The Heritage Language Question
This is one of the most frequent concerns I hear, and rightly so. The short answer: yes, there is a risk. Children who move abroad between ages 5–8 and enter environments where English is spoken at home too can lose Turkish as their dominant language. See this as a manageable risk, not a catastrophe. Conscious and consistent Turkish at home, reading Turkish books together, keeping a live connection to Turkish culture — these practices substantially reduce language loss risk. I always spoke Turkish with my children; it wasn't a rule, it was a choice. And that choice is today the foundation of both their identity and one of their strongest assets. 
## Family Profile: Is This Decision Right for You?
🟢 International schooling is likely a strong option if: Your child is curious and has a high capacity to adapt · Your family is already relocating abroad or has long-term international plans · Financial preparation is in place · University goals are global 🟡 Careful evaluation needed if: Your child has a very strong social network and may resist leaving · Your transition support system isn't yet established · The financial picture is uncertain · Language preparation hasn't started 🔴 Sending a child abroad alone (under 14): Separating children under 14 from their parents for international schooling carries significant psychological risks. This decision requires extremely careful evaluation — the child's personality and emotional maturity are decisive. Moving as a family is always the safer scenario. 
## Curriculum Choice: IB, A-Level or AP?
A practical guide to the most common international curricula: IB (International Baccalaureate) — the widest university acceptance network globally. The strongest passport to prestigious universities in Europe, North America and Asia. Research and critical thinking focused. A-Level — the UK standard. First choice for UK and Commonwealth university applications. Deep but narrow — strong subject focus, less breadth. AP (Advanced Placement) — integrated with the US university system. A strong option for families targeting American higher education. On returning to Turkey: YÖK recognises IB, IGCSE/A-Level and AP qualifications and conducts equivalency assessments for foreign high school diplomas, giving qualifying graduates the right to university placement. ## Decision Checklist
Before you decide, honestly answer these: Have you had an honest, age-appropriate conversation with your child? Is your school target and curriculum preference clear? Have you calculated the full financial picture — school fees + living costs + preparation? Is a language preparation plan in place? Have you researched the return scenario and equivalency process? Have you assessed your child's social and emotional readiness? Is there a plan for maintaining Turkish language and cultural identity? The most common mistake: treating international schooling as a prestige signal. Decisions driven by "the neighbour's child studies in London" typically cause significant stress within 2–3 years — because your child's real needs, personality and your family's actual life plan are entirely different from anyone else's. The right decision is your decision — made consciously, for your child and your family.

### What is the best age to move abroad with children for schooling?
Ages 3–10 offer the easiest language and social adaptation. Children in this window typically reach near-native English fluency within 12–18 months. Moves at 10–13 are very manageable with proper planning. Adolescent transitions (14+) require significantly more preparation, emotional support and typically a structured language course before the move. 
### How do I choose between IB, A-Level and AP?
Start with your target university region: UK/Commonwealth → A-Level; global or European universities → IB; US universities → AP or IB. Then consider your child's learning style — IB is broader and more research-focused; A-Level is deeper in fewer subjects. If you're genuinely undecided, IB is the most flexible choice because it's accepted everywhere. 
### Will my child lose their Turkish?
There is a real risk, particularly for children aged 5–8 moving into English-dominant environments. The mitigation is conscious effort: speak Turkish at home consistently, read Turkish books together, maintain cultural connections. Families who make this a deliberate practice rather than an afterthought overwhelmingly preserve their children's Turkish. 
### What are the real total costs of international schooling?
School fees vary widely by destination: Dubai international schools run AED 40,000–120,000/year; UK independent schools £15,000–50,000/year; US private schools $25,000–60,000/year. Add cost of living, language preparation, uniform, activities and boarding — the full-year budget is typically 40–60% higher than tuition alone. See our International Education Cost Comparison → 
### If we return to Turkey, will the foreign diploma be recognised?
Yes — YÖK conducts equivalency assessments for foreign high school diplomas and recognises IB, IGCSE, A-Level and AP qualifications. Qualifying students receive the right to university placement in Turkey. Start the equivalency process as early as possible; the paperwork takes time. Keep certified translations of all school documents throughout your time abroad. ## [My Child Is Shy and Insecure: Building Confidence](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/shy-and-insecure-child/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/shy-and-insecure-child/  
**Date:** 2026-10-14

14 October 2026 Ozlem Cimen 11 min read Summary In this article: the difference between shyness and low self-confidence, how confidence is eroded at home without us realising, and why the most durable path is to build on a child's strengths rather than patch their weaknesses. 
# My Child Is Shy and Insecure: Building Confidence Through Strengths
Shy child Insecure child How to build confidence in a child Child won't participate in class The child standing in the corner at a birthday party, clinging to you instead of joining the game. The student who knows the answer but won't raise a hand when the teacher asks. The little one who says "I can't do it" before even trying. Watching these moments, your heart sinks — because you know how capable your child really is, but they can't seem to see it themselves. Low confidence is one of the things parents worry about most and feel least able to "fix." You can make a study plan to raise a grade, but no one tells you exactly how to raise confidence. The good news: confidence is not a fixed, innate trait. It can be built in the right conditions — and the most solid foundation for that build is not where most parents look. Let me say one thing up front: low self-confidence is not a character flaw. Labels like "timid," "shy," or "withdrawn" describe but explain nothing. And some of those labels aren't even low confidence. Let's start there. 
## Shyness or Low Confidence?
This is the most frequently confused — and most harmful — distinction. Introversion (shyness) is a temperament; low self-confidence is a belief. An introverted child draws energy from quiet, from reflection, and from a few close relationships. In a crowd they hang back, observe first, then join in. This is entirely healthy and not something to be changed. An introverted child can be perfectly self-assured — they just don't broadcast it loudly. Low self-confidence is different: it is the belief "I am inadequate, I can't, I won't manage." A child can be both extroverted and insecure, or both introverted and confident. Making this distinction is critical, because pushing an introverted child to "be more social, don't be shy, speak up" sends the message that who they are is not enough — which turns healthy shyness into genuine insecurity. First ask: is my child simply quiet, or are they withdrawing out of an "I can't" belief? The first is temperament; the second is a belief worth supporting. 
## The Signs of Low Confidence
Genuine low confidence shows up through these markers: Giving up before trying: faced with a hard task, they say "it won't work anyway" and quit before starting. Constant approval-seeking: at every step, "like this?", "did I do it right?"; they don't trust their own judgement. Unable to own success: when they do well they say "it was easy" or "just luck" — never that it came from them. Disproportionate reaction to mistakes: a small error brings excessive distress, embarrassment, sometimes tears. Negative comparison: they constantly measure themselves against peers and always see themselves as falling short. If these appear together and persistently, the issue is confidence, not temperament. The good news: these signs usually share a single root — and that root can be addressed. 
## Where Is Confidence Eroded?
Parents love their children and want the best for them. But some well-intentioned things quietly wear confidence down. Listing them is not to blame — it's to see the loop. 
### Comparison
"Your brother could do this at your age," "look how nicely your friend presented" — these don't motivate; they tell the child "you're inadequate." Comparison, especially between siblings, is where confidence erodes fastest. 
### Outcome-Focused Praise
"Well done, you got 100!" praises the result. Over time the child learns: my worth depends on my grade. This produces a child who works from fear of failure and avoids risk. In contrast, process praise — "you didn't give up until you solved that, I noticed" — feeds effort and resilience. 
### Unnoticed Strengths
Most children grow up constantly "developed" in areas they aren't strong in, while the areas where they genuinely shine go unnoticed. A child who struggles in maths but is a remarkable storyteller — if named all year only by the maths gap — learns to define themselves as "a child who is lacking." This is confidence's most insidious enemy. 
### Over-Protection
Speaking for the child, solving problems on their behalf, removing every situation that might be hard — these are expressions of love, but they carry a hidden message: "you can't cope on your own." Confidence is built through the experience of overcoming small difficulties oneself. 
## 5 Ways to Support Confidence at Home
Praise the process, not the result: name the effort, the strategy, the patience. "How did you do it?" is more valuable than "what did you get?" Give small areas of autonomy: let them make their own choices (clothes, weekend plan, which homework to start with). Making choices feeds "I can decide." Normalise mistakes: share your own. "I got something wrong today, then fixed it." A child who sees that mistakes are safe isn't afraid to try. Name their strengths: "you're so curious," "you really understand people," "you finish what you start" — concrete strength feedback builds a positive self-image. Stop comparing: compare the child only to their own past self: "you're doing this more easily than last month." 
## The Foundation of Durable Confidence: Strengths
Now to the most important point. The clearest thing I've seen in years of working with students: confidence lasts when it's built on strengths, not by trying to patch weaknesses. When a child has the experience "I'm good at this" in their strongest area, that feeling spills into other areas. A child who feels competent in their strength is more willing to try in areas they struggle with — because the centre of their identity now holds "someone who is genuinely good at some things" rather than "I'm inadequate." So what exactly are a child's strengths? Most parents sense them but can't see them systematically. This is where the framework of character strengths helps: it measures 24 character strengths (curiosity, creativity, perseverance, kindness, honesty, hope and more) to reveal a child's signature strengths. Here's an example profile. #### Areas to Develop

Starting from that profile and creating opportunities to use those strengths feeds confidence at the level of behaviour. 
## Confidence at School: Working With the Teacher
For a child who won't participate or avoids presenting, the most effective step is a quiet partnership with the teacher. You can ask that the child be called on for a question they prepared and feel sure about. The first positive experience — "I raised my hand, I got it right, nothing bad happened" — breaks the fear. A few small wins and participation starts to grow on its own. It also helps to share the child's strengths with the teacher. A teacher who knows the child not only by the subject they struggle with but also by where they shine will create moments that make the child feel valued. This is the most productive way to put a child's strengths and weaknesses to work with the school. 
## When to Seek Professional Support
Home approaches make a difference in most cases. But when low confidence is tangled up with academic decline, it gets hard to tell: is the child withdrawing because they're struggling, or struggling because they've withdrawn? There are two routes. First, see the child's true academic standing objectively — when that is clear, you can see how much of "I can't" comes from a real gap versus lost confidence. Second, academic coaching focuses on restarting the confidence loop through small wins built on the child's strengths. If the confidence problem also affects sleep, eating and friendships and lasts for weeks, a child-and-adolescent psychologist should be involved. Discover your child's signature strengths. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### How does confidence develop in a child?
Confidence grows from competence and feeling valued — not from praise. A child's confidence rises when they achieve something through their own effort and that effort (not the result) is noticed. The most durable path is to name a child's natural strengths — curiosity, creativity, kindness, perseverance — and create opportunities to use them. Constantly trying to fix weak areas lowers confidence; starting from strong areas raises it. 
### Is shyness (introversion) the same as low self-confidence?
No. Introversion is a temperament — the child draws energy from quiet and a few deep relationships — and it is completely healthy. Low self-confidence is the belief "I can't, I'm not good enough." An introverted child can be quiet in a crowd yet fully self-assured. Forcing an introverted child to be "outgoing" damages their confidence. The goal is not to change the child but to help them feel strong in their own way. 
### My child won't participate or raise their hand in class; what should I do?
Not participating usually comes from the fear "if I answer wrong I'll be embarrassed." Lower the pressure: instead of asking "why don't you participate?", work with the teacher so the child is called on for a question they prepared and feel sure about. At home, build the habit of voicing opinions with "what do you think?" instead of right-or-wrong questions. Seeing that mistakes are part of learning — and that you make them too — reduces the fear. 
### What are the signs of low self-confidence?
Common signs: avoiding new or hard tasks, giving up before trying, constantly seeking approval, being excessively upset by small mistakes, comparing themselves unfavourably to peers, and attributing success to luck. These are not character flaws — they usually signal that the child's strengths have gone unnoticed and that they are being compared on the wrong terms. EduBot EduBot ✕

# Moving Abroad During High School: How Will My Teen Adjust, and How Is the University Journey Affected?
moving abroad high school IB transfer high school AP system university application abroad Moving to a new country is full of uncertainty even for adults; for a high-school student in search of identity , with friendships at the centre of their life, it is a far deeper turning point. At Edualist, the question we hear most often from our families — the one that tugs most at their hearts — is always the same: "If my child moves abroad during high school, will they be cut off from their social circle and left alone? Most importantly, how will their future and university success be affected by this process?" Let's take a close look at both the delicate periods this important transition can bring, and at how, with the right guidance, it can turn into an enormous advantage that enriches your child's life. 
## 1. Social and Emotional Adjustment: The Importance of the First 6 Months
The high-school years are when a young person's need to feel they belong is at its highest. Leaving behind their school at home, the routine they're used to and their childhood friends can create an initial sense of "loss." Understanding a New Culture: the first few months of a move can show up in teenagers as withdrawal, homesickness or adjustment fatigue. These emotional swings are entirely natural and need to be lived through. To understand the broader effects of the digital age on adolescent mental health, you can also read our article on The Anxious Generation: teen mental health . Language and School Culture: however well your child knows the foreign language, getting used to the social dynamics and slang among their peers will take some time. After the warm, close school climate many are used to at home, the more reserved manner in some countries can feel foreign at first. Ozlem Cimen — Our Approach The most valuable key in this process is patience. Easing the academic pressure on the child in the first months, and making room for them to join out-of-school sports clubs, art activities or communities they're interested in, helps them cross the language barrier organically and build lasting friendships. 
## 2. Changing Education Systems: The Right Timing in Curriculum Choices
Moving from the exam-focused system at home to systems abroad based on projects, analytical thinking and process assessment requires a serious mental shift. The most critical question in planning here is: at which stage of high school is your child joining this new system? In international programmes, course choices and academic strategies differ according to the curriculum you choose : 
### The AP (Advanced Placement) System
In the American system, the academic foundation and course choices start as early as Grade 9. Because the course marathon and exam planning that strengthen a university application take shape from the very first year of high school, families aiming for AP need to draw a much earlier and more deliberate roadmap. In the UAE, see our guide to the best AP schools in Dubai . 
### The IB (International Baccalaureate) System
In the IB programme, Grade 10 is a vital bridge. Because the final two years of high school (Grades 11 and 12) determine everything. Which subjects a student takes at Higher Level (HL) in Grade 11 depends entirely on teacher feedback and in-school guidance during Grade 10. For a British alternative, compare the A-Level schools in Dubai . Whatever the curriculum, the early years of high school are a critical window of flexibility for the teen to work out the new school's expectations, make peace with the system and make course choices on time. When a student starts Grade 11 already familiar with the system and with a clear course map, they can get through those two most intense years with minimum stress and maximum focus. 
## 3. How Is the University Journey Affected?
With the right strategy and steps that nourish the child's potential, when this move is managed professionally it exponentially increases their chance of being admitted to a world-class university. 
### The Biggest Advantages It Can Offer
Holistic Assessment: universities abroad don't measure students by a single three-hour exam. The projects a student develops throughout high school, their community work and personal interests play a huge role in admissions. Freed from exam pressure, the teen explores their own potential more freely. Local Student Status: in some countries, students who complete the final years of high school there can be assessed as "local students" rather than "international students" in university applications. This can both increase the chance of admission and optimise education costs. 
### Risks to Watch For
GPA Balance: in the first year, grades may dip temporarily due to unfamiliarity with the system. But there's no need to panic; selective universities worldwide see the first-term adjustment dip of a newly arrived student and look favourably on the upward trajectory shown in the following months. 
## Let's Make the Journey Better, Together
A young person moving abroad during their high-school years gains a global vision they will carry for life, a foreign language at near-native level, and the chance to open the doors of world universities. The most important thing in this process is to take the right steps from the very start to ease the child's academic and emotional load. With the right school choice beginning before the move, course and curriculum matching, and a preparation process that puts the child's world at its centre, it is possible to come through this big change with zero damage and lasting success. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does moving abroad during high school affect university applications?
Yes, significantly. Transferring into the IB Diploma or A-Level programmes during high school in particular requires strategic planning for university admissions calculations and scholarship applications. The right timing can increase career opportunities. 
### How long does a high-school-aged child's adjustment abroad take?
Academic adjustment usually takes 1-2 semesters, while social and emotional adjustment ranges from 6 to 18 months. Language support, the right school choice and the family's approach directly shape this process. 
### Which curriculum is most suitable for transfers during high school?
The IB programme is the most flexible option for high-school transfers, as it brings students from different countries into a common framework. Recognition of existing courses and credit transfer happen most easily in the IB system. 
### How does changing school during high school affect university applications?
A school change in Year 9 or 10 can positively affect a university portfolio. However, moving in Year 11 or 12 can be risky because of differences in exam systems. For this reason, the end of Year 10 is the ideal transfer point. 
### When is the hardest period for teens who move abroad during high school?
Research shows the first 6-9 months are the hardest period. The language barrier, the lack of a social network and the pressure of academic adjustment are all experienced at once. Early support (coaching, language support, social activities) shortens this period. EduBot EduBot ✕

## [Third Culture Kids (TCK): A Parent's Guide](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/third-culture-kids-guide/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/third-culture-kids-guide/  
**Date:** 2026-10-14

14 October 2026 Ozlem Cimen 11 min read Summary A comprehensive guide to the identity, belonging and adjustment journey of Third Culture Kids growing up across several countries — including family strategies and ways to strengthen a TCK identity. 
# Third Culture Kids (TCK): Identity, Advantages and Challenges
third culture kids TCK raising kids abroad expat child psychology identity confusion reverse culture shock Children growing up abroad find themselves in a place that's hard to define. They belong neither fully to their parents' culture nor to the country they live in. This in-between place is called the "third culture." And the children who live this experience are called TCKs — Third Culture Kids. Ozlem Cimen — A note from the coach My own children are TCKs. They grew up in different countries, different schools, different circles of friends. The first time they asked "Where do I belong?" in tears, I didn't know what to answer. I wrote this guide as a mother who lived those moments, and later as a coach who has walked alongside hundreds of families through the same thing. Coined in the 1960s by the American sociologist Dr Ruth Hill Useem, the term applies to far larger numbers today. As the world becomes more global, TCKs multiply. In cities like Dubai, 90% of the population is made up of expat families. TCK definition: children who spend a significant part of their childhood years in a culture different from their parents' — and, as a result, feel they belong fully neither to the parental culture nor to the culture of the country they live in. 
## TCK Advantages: The "Superpowers"
🌍 Cultural Intelligence Because TCKs internalise more than one culture, they easily develop mutual understanding. Seeing different perspectives becomes natural to them. 🗣️ Language Ability Exposure to several languages in childhood makes learning additional languages far easier. Less accent, higher fluency. 🔄 Adaptability Constant change makes TCKs adaptive and resilient. Their ability to respond quickly in the face of crisis or difficulty is well developed. 💼 Career Advantage In global business and the diplomatic world, TCKs are sought after. They adapt rapidly to multicultural environments and build a wide international network. 
## TCK Challenges: The Real Stories
As much as the advantages, TCKs also face unique challenges. Parents can't support these children without understanding them. ❓ Identity Confusion "Who am I? Which culture do I belong to?" Many TCKs carry these question marks. Even the "what is your country?" box on a form can trigger a complicated process. 😔 A Deep Sense of Loss Each move changes friends, schools, daily life. TCKs may avoid making new friends, thinking "when will I have to leave anyway?" 🏠 Never Feeling "At Home" Back in their home country they may feel "but I live abroad." Abroad, the thought may be "but I'm from home." Hanging between two places can be exhausting. 📚 Reverse Culture Shock Returning to the home or passport country can create a new crisis. The child may have to live somewhere they no longer feel they "belong." 
## 5 Practical Strategies for TCK Parents
1. Have the Identity Conversation (Start Early) Talk honestly with your child: "We're from home, but right now we live here and you're growing up here. You've become part of both cultures. That isn't strange — it's a gift." Discuss the advantages and challenges of the TCK identity openly. 2. Preserve the Home Language — With Active Effort Set a rule of speaking your home language at home. A weekend "home-language only day," summer visits to the home country, online language classes. Consuming literature, film and music keeps the cultural tie alive. 3. Prepare in Advance for "Reverse Culture Shock" When a child raised abroad returns home, psychological preparation is essential. Talk beforehand: "Some things will be different back home. Making friends may take a little time — that's normal." Long return visits (months) are far more effective than short ones (weeks). 4. Model Your Own Adjustment The child watches your adjustment process. If, six months after moving, you're still saying "this place isn't mine," the child internalises that message too. Show your own adjustment and be a positive model for your child. 5. Give a Portable "Root" What TCKs need is not a single country or culture but a set of values they can carry. Preserving family values, personal ethics and cultural identity makes the child feel not "lost" but "someone who has choices." 
## Famous TCKs
Barack Obama, Kobe Bryant, Lupita Nyong'o — all TCKs. In cities like Dubai, millions of children live a similar experience. Managed consciously, this difference can make a child one of the most well-equipped people in the world. Talk to your child about the TCK identity early Preserve the home language with deliberate effort Prepare psychologically in advance for returns Model your own adjustment for your child Build a portable value set, independent of any one country 
## From Home to Abroad: Easing the Transition Period
How the transition period is managed is critical to the healthy development of a TCK identity. Research shows that maintaining certain rituals and habits during a move significantly increases children's speed of adjustment. Especially in the 8-14 age group, preserving connections to the home country matters greatly when moving to a new one. Video calls, shared online games and return visits over the summer keep that connection alive. Framing it not as "leaving home behind" but as "adding a new layer" supports the child's identity development. Practical tip: before the move, make a "memory box" from home with your child. Photographs, small objects and notes from friends go inside. On hard days, that box can serve as a powerful emotional anchor. 
## Identity Crisis in TCK Children: Signs and Solutions
A TCK identity crisis usually shows up through questions like: "Where am I from?", "Which football team should I support?", "Am I from home, or from here?" These questions are a natural part not only of adolescence but of growing up multicultural. To view the social and digital factors affecting adolescent mental health in this period from a broader perspective, you can also read our article on The Anxious Generation: teen mental health . In this period, the parent's most valuable contribution is to accompany the question rather than answer it. When "you can be both" is reinforced with "you don't have to choose one," children integrate far more quickly. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a third culture kid (TCK)?
A third culture kid (TCK) is a child who spends a significant part of their developmental years in one or more countries different from their parents' culture. They develop a unique identity nourished by several cultures but not fully belonging to any one of them. 
### What are the most common challenges TCKs face?
The most common challenges include identity uncertainty, a constant sense of goodbye and loss, a feeling of rootlessness, and the search for belonging during adolescence. At the same time, being multilingual, culturally flexible and globally minded are among a TCK's greatest strengths. 
### How can parents support their TCK children?
Effective strategies include building a strong family culture, documenting memories from each country, preparing emotionally for frequent goodbyes, and connecting with TCK communities. 
### What advantages do third culture kids have in adulthood?
TCK adults typically have higher cross-cultural empathy, multilingual communication skills, and the capacity to build a global professional network. Research shows TCK individuals perform above average in international career environments and adapt more easily to leadership roles. 
### What stages does TCK identity development go through?
According to David Pollock's model, TCK identity development has five stages: leave-taking, transition, chaos, settling in, and re-involvement. This cycle is relived with every move and shapes the child's emotional processing capacity. EduBot EduBot ✕

# Turkey Sends 46,000 Children Abroad Every Year — The Truth Behind the Number
Turkey emigration statistics Turkish children abroad family relocation data brain drain Turkey Summary According to TÜİK data, Turkey sends 46,399 children and young people abroad every year across the 0-22 age range. What's behind this number, which age group is affected most, and how should families prepare for this journey? Last month I ran into a former colleague at a coffee meeting in Dubai. Years ago we worked at the same school together; she had since left and moved to the Netherlands with her two children. "How did you decide?" I asked. Her answer was simple: "I didn't really decide — the numbers decided. I saw what growing up here would give my kids, and there was no going back." That conversation brought back a question I'd been thinking about for a while: how many children and young people actually leave Turkey every year? And what's the real story behind that number? The answer is bigger than most people guess. According to TÜİK (Turkish Statistical Institute) data, Turkey sends 46,399 children and young people abroad every year across the 0-22 age range. That's close to the population of a mid-sized Turkish district — and it happens again every single year. 
## What Do the Numbers Say?
TÜİK's international migration statistics show that the total population emigrating from Turkey each year is 151,140 people. Within that total, children and young people make up a surprisingly large share: roughly a third, or 46,399 people, fall within the 0-22 age range. This figure isn't a single block. It's made up of three distinct cohorts representing three very different life stages, each telling its own story: Age Group Annual Emigration The Story It Represents 0-14 years 18,136 Children moving with their families — the decision belongs to the parents 15-18 years 9,824 Teens relocating during high school or starting high school abroad 19-22 years 18,439 Young adults moving independently for university or career Total 46,399 The number that repeats every single year What's striking is that the smallest group, against expectations, is the 15-18 age range. This is largely because the high school years are seen as the "riskiest to relocate during" academically and socially — families either delay or move up the timing of a move to avoid this window. The two largest groups sit at opposite ends: young children (moved by family decision) and young adults (moving on their own). 
## What Drives These Families?
Having guided hundreds of families through this process, I consistently see three motivations behind these decisions: 1. The Globalisation of Educational Capital. Families increasingly see education not just as a local grade average but as internationally recognised "capital." An IB diploma, academic English proficiency, early preparation for international university admissions — all of these become an asset the child carries wherever they choose to live in the future. 2. Merit and Employment Security. Many parents don't want their children to face the same career uncertainty they experienced themselves. They believe growing up in an environment with merit-based, transparent hiring processes offers a more secure long-term career foundation. 3. Social Welfare and Security. Beyond the education system, daily quality of life, access to healthcare, public safety and social welfare networks are also significant factors shaping the decision. Observation: Most of the families I work with describe their decision to relocate not as an "escape" but as an "investment." This framing significantly changes both family discussions and the child's own perspective on the process. 
## Not Every Child Makes the Same Journey
The migration experience of a 4-year-old and a 17-year-old, even on the same flight, are two entirely different journeys. Here's how the adaptation process tends to look by age: Age Group Language Adaptation Psychological Load Overall Assessment 0-6 years Very Easy Very Low Brain development is at its most flexible; highest chance of acquiring the new language like a native. 6-12 years Easy-Moderate Low-Moderate Academic language acquisition takes some time but social adaptation usually happens quickly. 12-18 years Difficult High The most sensitive period for identity formation and social belonging; requires comprehensive preparation and support. 19-22 years Moderate High Language load is lighter but identity and belonging continue to weigh heavily in a different way; individual support is essential. A neurobiological fact: The brain's flexibility for language acquisition declines with age, but this never means "impossible" at any age. The difficulty for the 12-18 age group isn't language — it's that social identity and belonging are at their most fragile during this period. 
## What Happens to Turkish?
One of the most commonly overlooked risks for families relocating abroad is the possibility of the child losing their native language. As children adapt quickly to a second language (usually English), Turkish can lose its fluency first, and then its vocabulary, as opportunities to use it outside the home shrink. The steps I recommend to reduce this risk are relatively simple but require consistency: speaking only Turkish at home, continuing to consume Turkish books and shows/films, making regular visits to Turkey, and connecting with Turkish communities abroad where possible. When deciding whether to school your child abroad , building this language-loss risk into the plan from the start is far more effective than trying to fix it later. 
## The Bigger Picture: What Is Turkey Losing?
The sum of individual family decisions translates into a demographic and economic picture at the national level. The 18,439-person 19-22 age cohort leaving every year is, to a large extent, a highly educated population segment that has completed or is about to complete university education. A portion of this group not returning represents a long-term loss of skilled workforce. This is also directly connected to the structural problems in Turkey's education system . A rote-learning-focused curriculum, frequently changing exam systems, and PISA results that lag behind international standards all directly shape the answer families give to the question "why should we stay?" The education system's own inability to improve indirectly fuels a cycle that strengthens the trend toward emigration. 
## What I Tell Families
I'd encourage you to read this not as a warning but as a call to prepare. Relocating abroad has become a statistically common choice, but every family's journey is unique. In practice, here's what I recommend: Prepare specifically for your child's age group. A social-emotional support plan for the 12-18 age group and language-enrichment opportunities for the 0-6 age group require very different priorities. Clarify the academic level before you move. Setting out without knowing which school, which year group, or which curriculum your child will start with makes the transition unnecessarily harder. Make Turkish part of the plan. Language loss is usually quite advanced by the time it's noticed; a preventive approach is always easier. Back the decision with data. Saying "I know" instead of "I feel" reduces family conflict and lowers the stress of the whole process. Behind these numbers are thousands of families and thousands of different stories. But they all share one thing in common: a relocation handled with the right preparation can become a gain in a child's life, not a loss. ## [Turkish School to Dubai School: Documents &amp; CAT4](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkey-to-dubai-international-school/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkey-to-dubai-international-school/  
**Date:** 2026-09-08

8 September 2026 Ozlem Cimen 12 min read Updated: 3 October 2026 Summary A relocation guide for Turkish families moving to Dubai: required documents, the official certification chain, what the CAT4 exam is, and how to prepare for school interviews — all explained clearly and concisely. 
# From Turkish Private Schools to Dubai International Schools 2026: Documents, CAT4 & Interviews
Quick Answer — What Documents Do You Need? Passport, visa, last 2 years' report cards (certified English translation), Transfer Certificate (authenticated via School → MEB → Apostille → UAE Consulate chain) and vaccination record. Start the process at least 2–3 months before your move — late starters miss application windows. For families with children, education planning sits at the top of every Dubai relocation list. Moving from Turkish private schools to Dubai international schools is an exciting step — but the registration process, paperwork and interviews can look complex. Here is everything you need to know, laid out clearly. Important: Document processes take time. Start at least 2–3 months before your move to Dubai. Families who start late miss application deadlines. 
## 1. Which Documents Do Dubai Schools Require?
All private schools in Dubai are regulated by KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority), which means enrolment standards are strict. Beyond the basic application documents (passport, visa, passport photo), the two most critical education documents are: 
### Required Education Documents
Last 2 Years' Report Cards: Your child's report cards must be translated into English by a certified sworn translator. Transfer Certificate (School Leaving Certificate): Every student enrolling in a Dubai school from abroad must present this document. It officially confirms which school your child left, which year group they were in, and that they are eligible to continue their education. 
## 2. The Document Authentication Chain
Official school documents from Turkey — especially the Transfer Certificate — must pass through a specific authentication chain before they are valid in Dubai. This takes time, so starting before your move is essential: 
### The 4-Step Authentication Chain
Step 1 — School Approval: The document must be written on the school's official headed paper and signed with a wet signature and stamp by the school principal. Step 2 — MEB Approval: The document must be certified by the District or Provincial National Education Directorate (İlçe/İl Milli Eğitim Müdürlüğü). Step 3 — Apostille: An Apostille / legalisation stamp from the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs is required. Step 4 — UAE Consulate Approval: Finally, the document must be endorsed by the UAE Embassy or Consulate in Turkey. Remember: All documents must be translated from Turkish into English or Arabic by a sworn translator before or alongside this authentication chain. 
## 3. What Is the CAT4 Test?
Most British, American and IB-curriculum schools in Dubai use the CAT4 (Cognitive Abilities Test 4) as part of their admissions assessment. CAT4 does not measure your child's accumulated knowledge or memory — it measures potential, reasoning ability and learning style . The test has four sections: 
### CAT4 Sections
Verbal Reasoning: Relationships between words and logical connections. Quantitative Reasoning: Numerical patterns and mathematical logic. Non-Verbal Reasoning: Problem-solving using shapes and visual patterns. Spatial Ability: Three-dimensional thinking and mentally rotating shapes. It is often said that "you can't study for CAT4" — but becoming familiar with the question formats and the logic of the test significantly reduces exam-day stress, especially for children sitting a test in a second language. Practising with sample questions is genuinely useful. Practical advice: CAT4 is conducted in English. Your child's familiarity with test instruction vocabulary — recognising what each question type is asking — directly affects their score. 
## 4. Primary and Middle School Assessment Processes
Assessment processes at international schools vary significantly by age group: 
### Primary School
Assessments are predominantly play-based . Rather than academic knowledge, the school observes the child's social adjustment and ability to follow instructions . Basic literacy and numeracy awareness are assessed. 
### Middle School
The CAT4 assessment is typically introduced at this level. Interviews with the admissions or guidance team assess the student's interests, hobbies and ability to express themselves . Adaptation capacity and potential to settle into a new environment are key factors. 
## 5. How Should Secondary Students Prepare for Interviews?
Secondary transitions are far more strategic because students are stepping into intensive programmes like IB Diploma, A-Level or AP . A critical point: in the AP system, course selections begin in Year 9. This means secondary interview candidates are expected to be able to articulate their academic goals and plans with some clarity, even at an early stage. 
### Secondary Interview Preparation Steps
Portfolio Presentation: Clubs in Turkey, sports achievements, MUN (Model United Nations) experience and social responsibility projects should all be highlighted in the interview. Autonomy: International schools expect students to take ownership of their own learning. Demonstrating this maturity in the interview is essential. Realistic Goals: Knowing which curriculum (IB, AP, A-Level) is the right fit and discussing it confidently with the school significantly increases admission chances. Ozlem Cimen — Coach's note The most common mistake I see in secondary interviews: the student is not prepared for "which university are you thinking of?" Answering "I don't know" to this question meaningfully reduces admission chances. Even if no firm decision has been made, a clear directional answer — "I'm considering engineering in the US" — is what's needed. 
## 6. Overcoming the Language Barrier
Transitioning to a fully English-medium education system is the biggest concern most families bring to me. But managing this process is less daunting than it looks: 
### 3 Ways to Bridge the Language Gap
EAL / ELL Support: Almost all international schools in Dubai have an EAL (English as an Additional Language) department. Students receive additional English language support during school hours, matched to their current level. Join Social Activities: Language barriers are broken on the pitch, not at the desk. Joining a sport, music group or arts club at school is the fastest route to learning English naturally through socialising. Summer Preparation: The summer before the transition is the ideal time to shift reading habits into English and build vocabulary before school starts. Dubai's education landscape is dynamic and the options are wide. From choosing the right school and preparing your documents to interview coaching and adaptation support — we are here for every step of this journey. We also recommend reading our guide on how children with limited English settle into Dubai schools . ### Do Dubai schools offer the same IB Diploma as Koç Okulu?

### What happens to Turkish language and identity at a Dubai international school?
Instruction is in English; Turkish isn't part of the curriculum. Many Turkish families in Dubai raise fully bilingual children; the risk exists but is not inevitable.

Most KHDA Outstanding schools accept international applications year-round. You'll need certified English translations of school transcripts, a reference from the previous school, and proof of UAE residency once you arrive. ## [Is There a Turkish School in Dubai? (2026 Guide)](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkish-school-in-dubai/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkish-school-in-dubai/  
**Date:** 2026-06-14

14 June 2026 Ozlem Cimen 6 min read Updated: 24 June 2026 
# Is There a Turkish School in Dubai? (2026 Guide)
Short Answer No. There is no school in Dubai that follows the Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB) curriculum. Turkish state schools exist in Qatar, Kuwait and Azerbaijan — but not in Dubai. That said, over 5,000 Turkish students attend Dubai's international schools , and weekend Turkish language classes are available through the Turkish Consulate General. When you decide to move to Dubai, one of the first questions that comes to mind is: "Which school will I send my child to?" And the question that follows almost immediately: "Is there a Turkish school in Dubai?" I've heard this from hundreds of Turkish families. I was surprised myself when I first learned the answer. Because Dubai has Indian schools, Pakistani schools, French schools. But there isn't a single school teaching the Turkish curriculum. In this post, I'll walk you through this reality — and more importantly, what to do about it. Ozlem Cimen — A note from your coach When we moved to Dubai, I had to face this reality head on. Everything I learned through that process, I'm sharing with you now — so you're not caught off guard. 
## Yes, There Is No Turkish School in Dubai
I want to be clear: as of now, there is no school in Dubai teaching the Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB) curriculum. There are Turkish schools in Qatar, Kuwait, and Azerbaijan — but not in Dubai. What does this mean in practice? When your child starts school in Dubai, they won't receive Turkish-language education. Turkish history, Turkish literature, mathematics in Turkish — none of these will be part of the school curriculum. Is this a disaster? No. But being caught unprepared creates unnecessary stress for both you and your child. I experienced that unpreparedness firsthand. 
## So What Is Available in Dubai?
Dubai has over 210 private schools offering a wide range of curricula. The three systems most commonly chosen by Turkish families are: 
### British Curriculum
This highly structured, academically rigorous system leads to GCSE and A-Level qualifications. It's a strong choice if there's any chance your child might study in the UK or Australia later. That said, exam pressure begins at a relatively young age. 
### American Curriculum
A more flexible, project-based approach that gives children more room to develop at their own pace. If the US or Canada is on your radar, this is the natural choice. 
### IB (International Baccalaureate)
The system that offers the greatest advantage for international transitions. If your family may move to another country in the coming years — as most expat families navigate — IB schools make it much easier for your child to adapt anywhere . Fees tend to be higher. 
## How Will You Preserve Your Child's Turkish?
This is the truly important question. And it's the one most families overlook. In Dubai, your child will learn at school in English, speak English with friends, and live their social life in English. Without a conscious effort at home, Turkish weakens within 2–3 years. I've seen this with my own eyes. Steps I recommend to families for preserving Turkish: 1. Set a home language rule A rule to speak Turkish at home is simple but effective. Children resist at first — but it becomes routine. 2. Enrol in Dubai Turkish Hours Weekend Turkish classes are held under the Turkish Consulate General in Dubai, taught by Turkish teachers. These sessions are a solid support for maintaining your child's Turkish reading and writing. 3. Build a Turkish content habit Turkish books, Turkish series, Turkish podcasts. Language atrophies when it goes unused. 4. Keep the Turkey connection alive Spending summer holidays in Turkey, regular video calls with grandparents — these keep the language alive not just on paper, but through emotional connection. 
## What Is KHDA and Why Does It Matter?
A term you will inevitably encounter when choosing a school: KHDA. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) inspects and rates every private school in Dubai annually. Schools are evaluated across five categories from "Weak" to "Outstanding". Always check the KHDA report when evaluating a school. I recommend prioritising schools rated "Very Good" or "Outstanding". These reports are publicly available and free to access. You can also browse our guide to Dubai's best international schools . 
## For Families Who Say "My Child Doesn't Know English"
I hear this concern more than any other. And what I say immediately after is this: children learn far faster than adults. My own son had no exposure to school-level English when we arrived in Dubai. He struggled for the first few months, yes. But within a year he was speaking fluently with his friends. Language acquisition in children is a biological superpower — you just need to provide the right environment. That said, some schools are considerably better at language support than others. Always ask during school selection: "Do you have an English language support programme? How do you approach newly arrived students?" 
## If You Don't Know Where to Start
As a Turkish family about to relocate to Dubai — or one that has just arrived — the biggest challenge is trying to learn this entire system from scratch. ## [Is There a Turkish School in Germany? 2026](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkish-school-in-germany/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/turkish-school-in-germany/  
**Date:** 2026-09-14

14 September 2026 Ozlem Cimen 7 min read 
# Is There a Turkish School in Germany? (2026 Guide)
Short Answer Not in the traditional sense. There is no school in Germany that fully follows the Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB) curriculum. However, three meaningful alternatives exist: Türkiye Maarif Foundation schools in select German cities, weekend Turkish language classes run by Turkish consulates, and international schools in major cities. The vast majority of Germany's 3+ million Turkish-origin population sends children to German state schools. When Turkish families decide to move to Germany, one of the first questions is: "Is there a Turkish school in Germany?" For Dubai the answer was clear-cut: no. Germany is more nuanced, because Germany is home to the world's largest Turkish-origin community outside Turkey — over 3 million people. That scale inevitably creates some educational infrastructure. But understanding exactly what exists — and what doesn't — is critical before making school decisions. 
## Is There a Turkish School in Germany? The Direct Answer
There is no school in Germany that fully follows the Turkish Ministry of National Education (MEB) curriculum. MEB-affiliated Turkish state schools exist in Qatar, Kuwait and Azerbaijan — not in Germany. However, three meaningful alternatives do exist: 
### 1. Türkiye Maarif Foundation Schools
The Türkiye Maarif Foundation — established in 2016 as Turkey's official overseas education body — operates schools in select German cities. These don't deliver the full MEB curriculum but incorporate Turkish-language elements and maintain cultural connections with Turkey. Capacity is limited; not every city has one. 
### 2. Consulate Weekend Turkish Classes
Turkish consulates across Germany run weekend Turkish language and culture courses. These are supplementary, not full-time schools, but are a practical tool for maintaining Turkish literacy and cultural identity. Available in most major German cities. 
### 3. Turkish-Islamic Association Weekend Schools
DITIB and various Turkish associations run weekend Turkish and religious education programmes. No full academic curriculum, but useful for language and cultural preservation. 
## The German School System: What Turkish Families Need to Know
The biggest surprise for Turkish families arriving in Germany is how differently the school system works. The key structure: Grundschule (primary school): 4 years for all children. This is where German language acquisition happens. Gymnasium: Germany's university-track school, running from Year 5 to Year 12 or 13. Graduates receive the Abitur diploma, required for German university admission. Think of it as the academic equivalent of the Turkish Anadolu Lisesi — but typically more intensive. Realschule / Hauptschule: Vocational-track schools for students not directed towards Gymnasium. Gesamtschule: Mixed comprehensive schools that allow students to work towards Gymnasium-equivalent qualifications over time. Key insight: The Year 4 Gymnasium recommendation is one of the most consequential moments in a Turkish child's German education. Starting early academic support — especially in German — significantly improves the chance of a Gymnasium placement. 
## Preserving Turkish in Germany
The risk is real but manageable. Children who attend German schools, make German friends and live their social lives in German will naturally drift away from Turkish without conscious effort at home. Recommended steps: set a Turkish-only home language rule, enrol in consulate weekend classes, maintain regular contact with grandparents in Turkey, and build a Turkish-language media habit (books, series, podcasts). 
## Finding Türkiye Maarif Foundation Schools in Germany
The Türkiye Maarif Foundation operates schools in Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Cologne and Frankfurt, among other cities — and the network continues to expand. To find the nearest school, contact the Turkish Consulate in your city or check the Maarif Foundation's official website. Places are limited and demand typically exceeds supply in most locations. Apply as early as possible, ideally before the family relocation is finalised. 
## Bilingualism in Germany: A Long-Term Advantage
Research consistently shows that bilingual children — those who maintain active fluency in two languages — develop stronger executive function, cognitive flexibility and metalinguistic awareness than monolingual peers. For Turkish families in Germany, maintaining Turkish is not a compromise or a nostalgia project: it is a measurable cognitive advantage. Turkish-German bilingualism also opens university and career paths in both countries, including in Turkey's growing trade and diplomatic relationship with the EU. Bilingualism requires intentionality: it does not happen by accident. It requires a consistent home language strategy, community reinforcement and structured supplementary input. 
## Academic Preparation Before Moving
The most common mistake Turkish families make is underestimating the German language gap on arrival. Children who enter Grundschule (Years 1–4) with no German typically integrate within two to three years. Children who arrive at Year 5 — the Gymnasium selection point — face a substantially harder trajectory. If a move to Germany is planned, begin German language instruction in Turkey at least one to two years before the relocation date. Online German tutoring and A1/A2 children's language courses are widely available and effective when started early. # What Makes Turkish Students Succeed at Dubai International Schools?
Summary Turkish children shine every day in Dubai's international schools — some starting from zero English. Case one: a six-year-old girl who moved from Turkey to Dubai with zero English. She sat silently in class that first week — unable to understand her teacher, unable to talk to classmates. ## Turning the Language Barrier into an Opportunity
A child with limited English starting at a Dubai school looks daunting at first. But the numbers tell a different story: the vast majority of students in Dubai's international schools come from non-English-speaking families. Schools know this reality and are structured accordingly. Children aged 5–10 are the fastest group at language acquisition. At this age the brain internalises language patterns almost as a biological reflex. With a strong EAL (English as an Additional Language) programme , a conversational level within 6–12 months is entirely achievable. Children with a strong Turkish literacy foundation have an additional advantage here. Language transfer is real: a child who is a strong reader in Turkish picks up the English sound-letter relationship much faster. Our first case was a perfect example of this mechanism. 
## Academic Foundation: Turkish Education's Silent Advantage
The Turkish education system provides a strong base in mathematical thinking and numerical problem solving. Turkish children transitioning to IB PYP or British KS1/KS2 curricula in Dubai typically find themselves in the top quarter of their class in maths and sciences. This advantage becomes more visible as language develops. The child already understands the maths — they just couldn't express it in English yet. Most Turkish parents focus on their child's grade average. This is understandable — but it's an incomplete lens in Dubai's international school culture. In an international school, clubs, sports and arts activities serve three critical functions: they accelerate social network formation, keep the language alive in real contexts, and build self-confidence. Our second case makes sense precisely here: the drama club gave that twelve-year-old more than vocabulary — it gave him an identity, a sense of belonging. When these children reach leadership positions — class representative, club president, project lead — both language practice and the confidence cycle reinforce each other. And this profile makes a real difference in university applications years later.

## [Tutoring vs Academic Coaching: What's the Difference?](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/tutoring-vs-academic-coaching/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/tutoring-vs-academic-coaching/  
**Date:** 2026-10-17

17 October 2026 Ozlem Cimen 13 min read Summary In this article: what tutoring actually does — and doesn't do — what academic coaching solves instead, and how to work out which one your child genuinely needs. 
# Tutoring vs Academic Coaching: Knowing the Difference Saves Hundreds of Hours
Tutoring vs academic coaching Academic coach vs tutor When to use academic coaching Tutor or coach for my child For two years I paid for tutoring twice a week. The tutor was good — patient, clear, and easy-going with my child. After each session the homework was done. When exams arrived, the grades stayed exactly where they'd been before. At the end of year one I asked myself: "Why isn't anything changing?" At the end of year two I asked a different question: "Am I paying for the wrong thing?" The answer was yes. I was paying for the wrong thing. My child's problem wasn't a knowledge gap. The problem was study habits, time management, and an inability to apply what was understood. Tutoring fixes none of those things. I learnt that in week six of academic coaching — not in the two years of tutoring that preceded it. If you are about to ask that same question, this article is for you. 
## What Does Tutoring Do — and What Can't It Do?
Tutoring does one thing well: it closes knowledge gaps. It re-explains a topic that was taught poorly or not understood. It revisits a concept missed in class. It gives targeted support for a specific piece of homework or an upcoming test. That is an extremely valuable function — in the right situation. If a child has moved from one school to another and there are topics missing from the new curriculum, tutoring bridges those gaps. If important content was missed due to illness or travel, tutoring works well. If a teacher's explanation simply doesn't land for a particular child, a tutor offers a different angle. But there are situations where tutoring does not work, and knowing them is important. If the child understands the material but cannot apply it in an exam, tutoring doesn't help. If the child grasps the homework but can't bring themselves to start it, tutoring doesn't help. If the child cannot plan multi-week assignments in IB or A-Level, tutoring doesn't help. If the problem is motivation, tutoring doesn't help. The most dangerous trap tutoring creates is dependency. With the tutor present, everything gets done. When the tutor leaves, the child freezes. Sitting at the desk, nothing happens — because the habit formed is not learning, but waiting to be taught. Once that loop is established, it becomes hard to stop tutoring at all: take it away and nothing seems to happen, so it feels safer to keep it. Tutoring closes knowledge gaps. Academic coaching closes skill and system gaps. Confusing the two makes both ineffective. 
## What Does an Academic Coach Do — and What Can't They Do?
Academic coaching asks a completely different question: "Why can't this child work independently?" and "What does the child need in order to?" An academic coach does not teach subject content. In a coaching session you won't find explanations of quadratic equations or the causes of World War One. Instead a session looks like this: how much of last week's plan actually happened, what felt hard, what got in the way, what system could we build to get past that obstacle? Goals are set, concrete steps are planned, and the next session starts with accountability. Coaching produces strong results in these situations: the child understands the material but isn't working, or is procrastinating; the student is struggling to submit work on time in an intensive IB or A-Level programme; there is a motivation problem and no sustainable working rhythm; executive function skills (planning, organisation, prioritisation) are underdeveloped; the student has transferred to an international school and cannot adapt to the new system's expectations. But there are things coaching cannot fix either. If a child genuinely has never learnt the content — if fractions were never covered, if basic chemistry concepts are missing — coaching won't help there. A coach does not teach content. That content gap needs to be closed first. This is why, in some situations, both supports are needed together — but more on that below. What does a coaching session actually look like? It does not begin with "let me explain this topic to you." The coach asks: "Why didn't you do what you planned last week? What happened in that time? If the same situation comes up next week, what will you do instead?" These questions turn the child into an observer of their own behaviour — and that observation gradually becomes self-regulation. 
## Side-by-Side Comparison
Tutoring Academic Coaching Goal Teach content Build a system Session content Explanations, homework help Planning, feedback, goal-setting Outcome Short-term grade improvement Long-term independence Right situation Content gap Application, motivation, management When it falls short Creates dependency, builds no system Cannot work if content is zero Looking at that table, the two supports are not rivals — they answer different questions. The issue is never which one is "better," but which problem each one solves. 
## Which One Does My Child Need? 5 Questions
Before deciding, ask yourself these five questions. Each answer points you in the right direction. 1. Does the child know the material but not perform in exams? At home they answer questions correctly; in the exam the results don't come. This is not a content problem — it is an application and stress-management problem. Answer: Coach. 2. Is the topic genuinely not understood? When you try to explain, the child says "I don't know" and genuinely doesn't. Core concepts are missing. This is a content gap. Answer: Tutor. 3. Is the child completing homework but not improving test scores? Sitting at the desk, work gets done, but exam performance isn't shifting. There may be surface-level studying or a gap between doing and understanding. Answer: Coach. 4. Does the child understand with a tutor but can't work alone? This can be both a content issue and an independent-study issue. Some core concepts may not be consolidated, and at the same time there is no study system at home. Answer: Both — but in separate roles. Tutor for content, coach for systems. 5. Is there no study system at all? The child doesn't know when exams are, doesn't track deadlines, doesn't know where to start. This is an executive function problem. Answer: Start with a coach. 
## Why Tutoring Works Less Well in IB, A-Level, and International Schools
I want to answer this clearly, because it is the most common mistake I see at Edualist. IB and A-Level assessment, as IBO.org makes clear, does not test content knowledge alone — or at least not content knowledge in isolation. The IB Extended Essay is a three-thousand-word original research piece. What is assessed is depth of thought, source use, argument construction, and time management. Those skills are not developed through weekly tutoring sessions. A-Level coursework is a process that unfolds over weeks: the student must plan each next step, receive feedback, and revise. That requires planning and self-management skills — coaching, not tutoring. Compare this with exam-based systems like the Turkish national university exam (YKS), which are content-focused and test-technique-driven. Tutoring was designed for that model and works well within it. International programmes are skill-focused. Tutoring there is the wrong tool — like trying to hammer a nail with a screwdriver. This does not mean a student entering an international school or starting IB should never use tutoring — if there is a genuine content gap, tutoring fills it. But to manage the system, plan the programme, and meet submission deadlines, academic coaching is what is needed. 
## Can You Use Both Together?
Yes — but only if the roles are kept clearly separate. The most functional combination looks like this: a maths tutor closes content gaps; an academic coach builds the study system and time-management skills. Neither duplicates the other's work. The tutor does not try to coach; the coach does not try to teach. In practice, however, this separation blurs constantly. The tutor gradually starts having "motivational conversations." The coach gradually says "let me just explain this quickly." And you end up paying for both while both are doing the same thing. To prevent this, whenever you engage either support, ask one question: "What is this person's exact job?" Any session where the answer is unclear is probably wasting time and money. Using both together works — but only if the roles don't overlap. If your tutor is having motivational conversations and your coach is explaining content, both are in the wrong place. 
## A Practical Decision Tree: What to Do When
When you are unsure, follow these steps. First, observe. What does your child understand in class, and what do they do at home? Is homework being completed — and where does it stall? How are they preparing for exams, or not preparing? Then measure the real academic level. A school report grade does not reflect true level. Some children work above capacity just to stay at the class average — that is exhausting. Others appear below their real level because the material doesn't interest them. An EduEntry academic assessment measures genuine understanding and distinguishes which gaps are content gaps and which are system problems. Then decide. If the content gap is large, start with tutoring. If system and motivation problems dominate, start with coaching. If both are present, starting with coaching first is usually more effective — because without a working system, tutoring becomes inefficient anyway. A decision made without an assessment is a guess. And guesses cost years. An assessment gives you results in weeks.

### Tutoring vs academic coaching — which is better?
They solve different problems. Tutoring fills knowledge gaps; academic coaching addresses study systems, motivation, and time management. Without the right diagnosis, either can be a waste of money. 
### When should academic coaching start?
Before the problem becomes entrenched — ideally when starting a new programme or school. A student switching to IB or transferring to an international school benefits most from coaching in the first month, before a crisis develops. 
### Is tutoring pointless?
No. Tutoring is extremely valuable for genuine content gaps. It becomes ineffective when it is used to solve a skill or system problem — one that content delivery cannot fix. ## [UAE International School Guide: IB vs British](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/uae-international-school-guide/)
