10 June 2026 Ozlem Cimen 14 min read Updated: 3 October 2026 Summary A comprehensive guide to choosing among 1,600+ international schools in the UAE — comparing IB, British, and American curricula to help families find the right fit for their child. 
# UAE International School Guide: Everything You Need to Know
Quick Answer — UAE International Schools: The UAE hosts nearly 1,600 international schools with over 1.1 million students. Dubai schools are regulated by KHDA; Abu Dhabi schools by ADEK. The five main curricula are IB, British (IGCSE/A-Level), American (AP), French (Baccalauréat) and IPC. Annual fees range from AED 20,000 to 100,000+. The right school depends on where you work, where your child will go to university, and their learning style. The education landscape waiting for you when you move to the UAE is both exciting and overwhelming. With nearly 1,600 international schools and over 1.1 million students , the UAE hosts one of the world's largest and most diverse international education ecosystems. But that diversity brings a question: which school is right for your child? I have lived this system from the inside for years — both as an educator and as an expat parent. While my own children were in school in the UAE, I visited dozens of schools, spoke with parents and compared curricula. I wrote this guide to share that experience with you. Ozlem Cimen — Coach's note When we first moved to Dubai I had just a handful of school names to start with. As I researched, the lists grew and my head spun. Eventually I realised the most important thing was not "the best school" but "the right school for my child." These are two very different things. 
## Overview of the UAE Education System
Education in the UAE runs on two separate tracks: government schools (for Emirati nationals, taught in Arabic) and private international schools (designed for expat families, in various languages). As an expat family, the private track is almost always where you'll be looking. Dubai schools are regulated by KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority) ; Abu Dhabi schools by ADEK (Abu Dhabi Department of Education and Knowledge) . Both bodies inspect schools regularly and publish rating reports — the most reliable source for school selection. For a detailed guide to how Dubai's education system works, see our Dubai Education System guide . For Abu Dhabi schools, fees and ADEK ratings, see our Abu Dhabi International Schools guide . 
## Curriculum Options: Which Is Right for You?
Five major curriculum systems operate widely across the UAE. Each has different strengths, a different target student and a different university destination profile. 
### 1. International Baccalaureate (IB)
The UAE has 42 IB schools — one of the highest concentrations in the Middle East. The IB programme runs in three stages: Primary Years Programme (PYP), Middle Years Programme (MYP) and Diploma Programme (DP). IB emphasises critical thinking, academic writing and self-directed research. Universities in the US, Canada, UK and Australia view the IB Diploma as a strong qualification. Who is IB ideal for? Students who enjoy analytical thinking, who target more than one university system (US + UK + Australia) and who can handle academic pressure. Intensely demanding — not suited to every student. 
### 2. British Curriculum
The most common curriculum in the UAE. IGCSE (ages 14–16) and A-Level (ages 16–18) qualifications give students comfortable access to UK, American and Canadian universities. The British system is structured and exam-focused — students specialise deeply in 3–4 subjects at A-Level. Who is British curriculum ideal for? Students targeting UK, Canada or US universities who thrive in a structured, exam-based environment. The most popular choice among expat families. 
### 3. American Curriculum
Organised across elementary, middle and high school levels. AP (Advanced Placement) courses and SAT/ACT preparation provide a strong foundation for US university applications. Known for flexibility and a wide range of subject choices. Who is American curriculum ideal for? Students firmly planning to study in the US who prefer a flexible, project-oriented learning environment. 
### 4. French Curriculum
French lycées in Dubai and Abu Dhabi follow the French Ministry of Education programme, preparing students for the Baccalauréat exam. Teaching is in French; direct entry to universities in France and all Francophone countries is available. 
### 5. IPC (International Primary Curriculum)
Designed for ages 5–12, IPC takes a thematic, cross-cultural approach, prioritising curiosity and discovery over academic rigour. A good starting point for primary-age children at certain schools.

### Dubai
The UAE's largest and most diverse education ecosystem. Over 200 KHDA-regulated private schools — options for every budget and curriculum. Waiting lists at popular schools can be long: apply at least 12 months before your planned move . 
### Abu Dhabi
ADEK-regulated, smaller but high-quality ecosystem. Advantageous location for families working in government or energy sector roles. Some schools have ADEK-supported scholarship programmes. 
### Sharjah
Close to Dubai, with more affordable alternatives. Family-oriented character; school choice is more limited than Dubai. 
### Ras Al Khaimah (RAK)
For families seeking a quieter lifestyle. Established IB schools such as RAK Academy. Fees are noticeably lower than Dubai. 
## Application Process: Step by Step
Applications to UAE schools follow a standard pattern, though each school has its own specific requirements. Generally expected: Passport copy (child and parents) Previous school transcripts (last 2 years, with English translation) Vaccination record (complete and current) Health form (school-specific) Completed application form Interview or assessment (with the child at some schools, with the family at others) Ozlem Cimen — Coach's note Having transcripts with an Apostille and a certified English translation speeds the process up significantly. Getting a notarised translation done in Turkey before you arrive avoids delays. I strongly recommend completing this before you submit any application. For the full document authentication chain (School → MEB → Apostille → UAE Consulate) for Turkish school documents, read our comprehensive transition guide . 
## Choosing the Right School: A Practical Framework
An exercise I recommend to families before they start school searching: make a "must have" and "nice to have" list. Without keeping these two lists separate, you'll get lost in every school's glossy brochure. Must-have questions: What language will your child be taught in? Is their English preparation adequate? Which country are you targeting for university long term? Is your child young? Do they need a play-based or a structured environment? Do you want Arabic language instruction? (Required in UAE schools — check the hours.) Is the distance between school and home acceptable? Nice-to-have questions: Is there a swimming pool, arts studio or robotics club? Is school transport available? Is there a community of expat families? Golden rule: Go on a school tour. Not the website photos — the teacher-student interaction you observe in a real classroom tells you the truth. 
## Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Deciding on fees alone. The most expensive school is not necessarily the right one for your child. Curriculum fit and teaching quality are far more decisive. Mistake 2: Applying late. Waiting lists at popular Dubai schools can run 6–18 months. Apply as soon as your relocation decision is made. Mistake 3: Leaving your child out of the process. For children over 10, bring them to school visits. When they feel ownership of the school, the settling-in period is significantly faster. Mistake 4: Confusing curriculum with country. A "British school" follows the UK curriculum — but it's in Dubai. The school has no direct connection to a London, Sydney or Boston university. University applications are made separately. 
## Conclusion: Asking the Right Question
Choosing an international school in the UAE requires asking not "which school is the best?" but rather "which environment is right for my child?" These two questions can lead to very different answers. As an educator, I have analysed curricula for years. As an expat parent, I have lived this system from the inside. Every family's equation is different — but when families learn to ask the right questions, finding the right answer becomes much easier. # UK School Enrolment: Step-by-Step Guide for Turkish Families
The UK is home to one of the world's most established education systems. Names like Eton, Harrow and Wellington spring to mind — but school selection in Britain is far broader and more varied than most expat families expect. This guide walks you through the school system, the enrolment steps and the critical details to watch out for when moving to the UK with children. Note from Ozlem Cimen I watched my own children encounter the British education system for the first time. I've lived through what Ofsted ratings actually mean in practice, what the atmosphere of an independent school interview feels like, and how 11+ preparation affects the whole family. This guide distils those observations and hundreds of coaching sessions. Key dates: The UK academic year starts in September. State school applications open October–November ; independent school applications November–January . Late applicants almost always struggle to find places. 
## The UK School System: Four Main Options
Before choosing a school you need to understand the two fundamental categories — state schools and independent schools — and the sub-types within each. Type Cost Key feature State schools Free Quality varies by area; allocated by home address; rated by Ofsted Grammar schools Free State-funded but academically selective; require the 11+ exam; not available in every area Independent schools £15,000–£60,000+/yr Privately funded; smaller classes; strong extra-curricular programme; open to international students International schools £18,000–£35,000+/yr IB or American curriculum; most common in London; easiest transition for families arriving from abroad 
## Ofsted: The UK's School Inspection Body
Ofsted (Office for Standards in Education) inspects and rates state schools in England — similar to the role KHDA plays in Dubai. Schools are graded Outstanding, Good, Requires Improvement or Inadequate . Always read the Ofsted report before applying: all reports are free at ofsted.gov.uk . Independent schools are inspected by the ISI (Independent Schools Inspectorate) rather than Ofsted. Watch out: Property prices around "Outstanding"-rated state schools are often significantly higher. Decide on a school and a neighbourhood together — they're inseparable. 
## Curriculum Choice: GCSE/A-Level or IB?
The standard British curriculum runs GCSE (ages 14–16) then A-Level (ages 16–18). But IB Diploma and American AP programmes are increasingly common, especially in international schools. The key question for expat families: where do you want your child to go to university? UK or Commonwealth universities → A-Level is the strongest choice Europe, the US or global options → IB Diploma is more flexible and widely recognised If you're weighing IB against A-Level in detail, see our full curriculum comparison → 
## 8-Step Enrolment Process
Research your area — The city and neighbourhood you'll live in directly determines your school options. London, Manchester and Edinburgh all have far wider international school choices than smaller towns. Read Ofsted and ISI reports — For state schools use ofsted.gov.uk; for independent schools use the ISI website. Both are free and give you inspection judgements and detailed findings. Plan Open Day visits — UK schools typically hold open days in October and November. Visit two or three in person; classroom atmosphere and teacher interaction tell you things a website never can. Complete the application form — State schools: apply through your local council (Local Authority). Independent schools: apply directly to each school — every school has its own form and process. Prepare for entrance tests or interviews — Selective independent schools usually require the Common Entrance (CE) exam or their own entrance test. Grammar schools require the 11+. Allow at least 1–2 years of preparation. Gather your documents — Passport, visa/BRP card, school transcripts (translated into English by a certified translator), vaccination records and a reference letter from the previous school. Receive the offer and pay the deposit — Independent schools normally require a deposit within 1–2 weeks of an offer to secure the place. This is non-refundable if you later decline. Plan EAL and transition support — Choose schools that offer EAL (English as an Additional Language) provision matching your child's current level. Academic coaching in the first term is worth considering.

## Fees and Scholarships
State schools are free, though budget around £1,000–£3,000 per year for uniform, school trips and activities. Independent schools range from £15,000 to £50,000+ per year ; boarding schools sit at the higher end of that range. Scholarship tip: Many independent schools offer academic, arts or sports bursaries that can cover up to 50% of fees. Always ask when you apply — bursaries are rarely advertised prominently. 
## Boarding Schools
Boarding schools are one of Britain's most prestigious educational options. Schools like Eton, Harrow and Rugby offer both strong academic outcomes and deep personal development. However, for children aged 11–13 in particular, the boarding decision deserves very careful thought: your child's readiness and capacity to adapt should be at the centre of it. Experts generally advise against boarding for children under 7–8 years old. Annual costs run from £35,000 to £60,000+ .

### What happens if my child's English isn't strong enough?
Choose schools with dedicated EAL (English as an Additional Language) provision. Primary-age children typically adapt to English remarkably quickly — within 6–12 months. For secondary-age students, look for schools with structured language support programmes and consider a transition English course before term starts. 
### How are Turkish school grades assessed in the UK?
Transcripts must be translated into English and notarised. Some schools will run their own placement assessments regardless. Bring detailed mark sheets, not just summary reports — UK admissions teams want to see subject-by-subject performance. 
### Which city is best for families moving to the UK?
London has the widest school choice — state, grammar, independent and international — but the cost of living is substantially higher. Manchester, Edinburgh, Bristol and Bath all have strong schools and significantly more manageable living costs. Your choice of city should factor in commute, community and school availability together. 
### When do UK independent school scholarship exams take place?
Scholarship assessment exams are usually held in January–February, with results released in March–April. Applications for that cycle open the previous September–November. For 11+ and 13+ entry, start preparation at least 1–2 years in advance. 
### When does boarding school make sense?
Boarding is a strong option for families who move frequently or who want to build independence and self-discipline in their child. It works best for motivated students aged 13+. Annual all-in costs range from £35,000 to £60,000+. For younger children, a day school with strong pastoral care is usually a better foundation. ## [What Does an Education Coach Do?](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-does-an-education-coach-do/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-does-an-education-coach-do/  
**Date:** 2026-10-01

1 October 2026 Ozlem Cimen 7 min read Updated: 2 October 2026 Summary An education coach doesn't teach content — they build a learning system. This post breaks down what actually happens in a session, how coaching differs from tutoring, and which one you need using 5 real-life scenarios. 
# What Does an Education Coach Do? Tutor vs Coach — How to Choose
What does an education coach do Tutor vs coach Academic coaching session Education coaching "My child's grades have dropped — should I get a tutor or an academic coach?" Parents who ask this question usually share the same uncertainty: aren't they both just "help"? Why does it matter? It matters — and picking the wrong one without understanding what problem you're solving wastes both time and money. 
## What Does an Education Coach Do?
Short answer: An education coach doesn't look at what a student doesn't know — they look at how a student learns . They work on learning strategies, time management systems and academic confidence. Every session ends with a concrete action plan, which is reviewed at the start of the next session. More concretely, an education coach: Analyses the student's current study system and learning style Builds a personalised time management and prioritisation system Breaks large assignments and exam preparation into manageable steps Addresses exam anxiety and motivation blocks with practical tools Creates a weekly action plan and follows up at the next session Provides regular feedback to parents on progress 
## What Actually Happens in a Session?
A typical 30–45 minute session looks like this: Session structure (30-45 min): 1. Weekly check-in (5-10 min) — How did last week's plan go? Where did it break down? 2. Obstacle analysis (10 min) — Which subject, assignment or exam is causing difficulty this week? 3. Strategy work (15-20 min) — One specific skill or tool for that week (time blocking, active recall, exam simulation…) 4. Action plan (5 min) — 2-3 concrete, measurable steps to complete before the next session Note: there is no content teaching in these sessions. No maths problems are solved, no grammar rules explained. The entire session is about the student's system . 
## 5 Decision Scenarios: Coach or Tutor?
The fastest way to know which one you need is to ask the right question. These are the 5 scenarios I encounter most often: Scenario 1 — "Maths grades suddenly dropped" Likely a content gap — a specific topic wasn't understood. → Tutor is the faster fix. Scenario 2 — "Behind in every subject, doesn't know how to study" A learning system problem. Teaching content alone won't fix it. → Education coach . Scenario 3 — "Just moved to a new country or curriculum, everything changed" New system, new language, new expectations all at once. Not a content problem — an adaptation problem. → Education coach . Scenario 4 — "Works hard but gets no results" Effort exists; efficiency doesn't. The wrong strategy won't produce the right outcome. → Education coach . Scenario 5 — "Started IB or A-Level and is overwhelmed" IB in particular requires self-management and long-term project planning — unfamiliar structures for students from more exam-focused systems. → Education coach . 
## Tutor vs Education Coach: Side-by-Side
Tutor Education Coach Focus Specific subject content Learning system and habits What happens in sessions? Explanation, problem-solving Strategy, planning, follow-up Output Grade improvement in one subject A system that works across all subjects Duration of impact Short-term Long-term, transferable Best for Content gap, single-subject problem System problem, transition, motivation 
## How the Process Works
Coaching typically unfolds across three phases: Sessions 1-3 — Profiling: The student's learning style, strengths, challenges and goals are mapped. A short parent conversation is also included. Sessions 4-12 — Strategy building: Personalised strategies based on the profile are put into practice. Weekly action plans are created and consistency is tracked. Month 3 onwards — Independence: As coaching support gradually reduces, the student maintains their own system. The goal is a student who no longer needs a coach. 
## When Coaching Is Not the Right Fit
Education coaching is not the answer to every situation. Other approaches may be more effective when: There is a temporary dip in just one subject: A subject tutor will provide a faster, more targeted solution. An undiagnosed learning difficulty is suspected (dyslexia, ADHD etc.): A neuropsychological assessment should come first; coaching can be a supplement but is not the primary intervention.

### What does an education coach do?
An education coach works on learning strategies, time management and academic confidence rather than teaching subject content. Every session ends with a concrete action plan, which is reviewed at the next session. The goal is for the student to build an independent, efficient learning system. 
### Should I choose a tutor or an education coach?
If the problem is a specific subject's content, a tutor will solve it faster. If the problem spans multiple subjects, involves organisation, motivation or adapting to a new curriculum, an education coach is more effective. They solve different problems — neither replaces the other. 
### How quickly will I see results?
Sessions 1-3 are used to build the student's profile. Sessions 4-6 see strategies introduced and the first observable changes begin. Lasting habits typically take around 3 months (approximately 12 sessions). The pace of change depends on the student's motivation and consistency.

## [What Is a KHDA Rating? Ratings Explained](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-a-khda-rating/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-a-khda-rating/  
**Date:** 2026-09-24

Every private school in Dubai is inspected annually by KHDA and graded across four main categories. The rating is the most reliable official indicator of school quality — but it isn't the whole picture. This guide explains what each grade means, how inspections work, and how to use KHDA ratings when choosing a school. 
## What Is KHDA?
KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority) is the Dubai Government body responsible for regulating all private schools in the city. Its mandate goes beyond ratings: it covers school licensing, curriculum approval, teacher standards, and student safety. Each year — usually unannounced — a KHDA inspection team visits schools, observes lessons, reviews student performance data, and interviews senior leaders. At the end of the inspection, the school receives an official grade that is published on KHDA's publicly accessible website. Note: Schools in Abu Dhabi are inspected by ADEK (Abu Dhabi Department of Education and Knowledge), not KHDA. The system is similar but grades are not directly comparable. 
## The Four KHDA Grades
KHDA can assign six grades — but in practice, the vast majority of schools fall into these four categories: 
### KHDA Rating System
Outstanding The highest grade. Exceptional performance across all categories. Around 15–20% of Dubai schools hold this rating. Expect long waiting lists and higher fees. Very Good Strong performance. High scores across most categories with some room for growth. Many families' first-choice schools sit in this bracket. Good Solid performance by Dubai standards. Strong curriculum delivery, above-average student outcomes. Generally more accessible fees. Acceptable Meets minimum standards but with limited strengths. KHDA will require an improvement plan. Research carefully before choosing an Acceptable-rated school. Below these four grades sit Weak and Very Weak — schools in these categories face intensive KHDA monitoring and potential closure. I wouldn't recommend considering them for newly arriving families. 
## What Does KHDA Actually Measure?
The overall grade is not a single score. KHDA evaluates each school separately across four main areas: 
### 1. Student Achievement
Literacy, numeracy, and science performance; in-school assessment results; and outcomes in external qualifications (IB, A-Level, AP). This is the single most influential category in determining the overall grade. 
### 2. Quality of Teaching and Assessment
Lesson observations, classroom management, the quality of feedback given to students, and how well teachers personalise learning. 
### 3. Curriculum and Personal Development
Alignment between the school's curriculum and the authorising body's standards (Cambridge, IB, CBSE, etc.); contribution to students' social, emotional and personal development. 
### 4. Leadership and Management
Quality of senior leadership, teacher support systems, parent communication, safeguarding policies, and how effectively the school responds to KHDA recommendations. Full KHDA inspection reports are published free of charge at khda.ae/schools . Always read the full report before shortlisting a school — you'll find detailed strengths and areas for development that a summary grade doesn't convey. 
### Which KHDA grade is right for your child? Let's work it out
A rating alone doesn't tell you which school fits — book a free session to match your child's learning profile and goals to the right school. Book a Free Session 
## Outstanding vs Very Good: The Real Difference
This is one of the most common questions I hear. The short answer: both represent high-quality schooling, but there are two practical differences that matter. Waiting lists and competition: Outstanding schools — particularly GEMS Wellington, Jumeirah College , JESS — can have waiting lists stretching 1–2 years. Very Good schools typically require 6–12 months' lead time. Fee gap: Outstanding schools charge on average 20–35% more than Very Good schools. For a British curriculum Outstanding school in 2025–26, expect AED 70,000–95,000 per year; a Very Good equivalent typically sits in the AED 50,000–70,000 range. Viewed through the lens of your child's learning profile and your goals, a Very Good school is often as suitable as — and sometimes a better fit than — an Outstanding one. 
## Is a KHDA Grade Enough on Its Own?
No — and this is the most important point. A KHDA grade tells you about general school quality, not whether the school is the right fit for your child. Two schools with the same Outstanding grade can differ dramatically in curriculum (IB vs British), language support, class sizes, scholarship policy, and school culture. For a child who is new to English, a Very Good school with a strong EAL programme may be a better starting point than an Outstanding school without one. 
### What to Check Beyond the Grade
Inspection date Outstanding schools are inspected every 3–4 years. A 2021 grade and the school you're visiting in 2025 may not be the same school. Check the report date. Sub-category scores An overall Outstanding school may have scored Very Good in one sub-category (e.g. leadership). Read the full report, not just the headline grade. Curriculum fit IB, British, and American curricula suit different students. The grade doesn't tell you whether the curriculum suits your child. EAL / language support For a child still developing their English, the quality of the EAL (English as an Additional Language) programme is critical. This information is in the KHDA report. 
## Grade Distribution Across Dubai Schools
Based on 2024–25 data, there are more than 200 KHDA-licensed private schools in Dubai. The approximate grade distribution is: Outstanding: ~35–40 schools (17%) Very Good: ~70–80 schools (36%) Good: ~65–75 schools (32%) Acceptable and below: ~30 schools (15%) Around 85% of students in Dubai attend a school rated Outstanding, Very Good or Good — a sign that the overall standard of private education in the city is high. 
## Which Grade Is Right for Your Family?
Here's a practical framework based on budget and your child's profile: Outstanding: Strong academic ambitions, competitive budget, starting your school search 18+ months before the target start date Very Good: High quality, more accessible fees, 6–12 months' lead time — the ideal balance point for most families Good: Solid education, budget-friendly, flexible availability; a good entry point for newly arrived students adjusting to a new environment Worth knowing: "Outstanding" has become something of a marketing label. Check whether the school's standout features that impressed you in the prospectus actually appear as strengths in the KHDA inspection report.

## Frequently Asked Questions
What is a KHDA rating? KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority) is Dubai's official school regulator. It inspects every private school and assigns one of six grades: Outstanding, Very Good, Good, Acceptable, Weak, or Very Weak. The grade reflects academic quality, teaching standards, curriculum delivery, and student welfare. What is the difference between Outstanding and Very Good? Outstanding schools demonstrate exceptional performance across all KHDA categories, with student outcomes in the top 10% of international benchmarks. Very Good schools show strong performance but don't quite reach Outstanding in every area. In practice, both represent high-quality schooling; the main difference shows up in waiting-list length and fee levels. How often does KHDA inspect schools? Outstanding schools are inspected every 3–4 years, Very Good schools every 2–3 years, and lower-rated schools annually. This means a school's current grade may be several years old — always check the inspection date alongside the grade. Is KHDA Good a good grade? Yes — KHDA Good represents solid and satisfying performance by Dubai standards. Good-rated schools deliver the curriculum well, prioritise student welfare, and typically offer more accessible fees than Outstanding schools. Depending on your child's needs and your budget, a Good-rated school can be an excellent choice. ## [What Is an Academic Coach? Definition & Role](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-an-academic-coach/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-an-academic-coach/  
**Date:** 2026-09-30

30 September 2026 Ozlem Cimen 8 min read Updated: 4 October 2026 Summary An academic coach doesn't teach subjects — they teach students how to learn. This post explains what academic coaching is, how it differs from tutoring and school counselling, and the key signs that your child needs one. 
# What Is an Academic Coach? How They Differ from Tutors — and When You Need One
"We already have a private tutor — twice a week — but the grades just aren't moving." This is one of the most common things parents say to me. The issue is rarely the tutor's quality. The deeper gap is that the child hasn't yet learned how to learn . That gap is exactly what an academic coach closes. 
## What Is an Academic Coach?
An academic coach is a specialist who doesn't teach subject content — they teach the process of learning itself . The question is never "how do you solve this equation?" It is "how do you develop the habit of solving this type of problem reliably, across every subject, under pressure?" What an academic coach works on: Building learning strategies tailored to the individual student; constructing a personalised time management system; structuring study habits that actually stick; developing exam anxiety management skills; uncovering genuine sources of motivation; and establishing weekly action plans so the student increasingly manages their own progress — independently. 
## How Is an Academic Coach Different from a Private Tutor?
These two roles are frequently confused, but their purposes are fundamentally different. A private tutor focuses on the content of a specific subject. They explain the maths problem, clarify the grammar rule, make sure the formula is memorised. This is short-term and topic-specific. After the session, the student is left with the answer to that particular question. An academic coach never delivers subject content. Instead, they give the student the systems and tools that work across every subject: how to set priorities, how to break large assignments into manageable steps, how to sustain attention, how to process feedback constructively. These are skills that travel — from the maths exam to secondary graduation, into university and beyond. For a closer look at how a coaching session actually unfolds — and the concrete scenarios that separate a coach from a tutor — see our piece on what an education coach does . A tutor gives your child a fish. An academic coach teaches them to fish — and then to choose the right lake and equipment. 
## How Is an Academic Coach Different from a School Counsellor?
A school counsellor operates in an institutional role: managing timetables, monitoring grades, intervening in crises. Their frame of reference is the school's interests and expectations. An academic coach works solely in the student's interest . In a focused 30-minute session built on genuine trust, the coach explores how the student is actually feeling, where they are genuinely stuck, and what they privately don't believe about themselves. They then work through those blocks together. They also stay in communication with the family, ensuring continuity of support outside the sessions themselves. 
## When Does a Child Need an Academic Coach?
Watch for these signs: Your child studies for long hours but grades don't improve They've moved to a new country or curriculum (IB, A-Level) recently Exam periods trigger disproportionate stress and anxiety Homework and projects routinely get left until the last minute Motivation is low — "I just can't do it" has become a fixed belief Strong in one subject, completely disengaged in all others If one or more of these patterns is present, the underlying issue is almost never a lack of intelligence or effort. It is that systematic learning skills have never been explicitly developed . Academic coaching intervenes at precisely this level. 
## Academic Coaching for International School Students in Dubai
Students in Dubai's international schools face a particularly demanding combination: a new country, a new language of instruction, and a curriculum — IB or A-Level — that operates very differently from the Turkish exam-based system many of them came from. Managing all three simultaneously is genuinely hard. Success in international schools comes not just from subject knowledge, but from a structured learning system, time management and adaptation to the school culture . Strengthening all three dimensions at once is the core of academic coaching. Students entering IB for the first time will also find our guide on academic coaching during the IB transition directly relevant. Wondering whether your child fits this profile? Our article on why high-achieving students struggle with IB explores the patterns in depth — and what to do about them. Ready to take the next step? ## The Research Evidence for Academic Coaching
Academic coaching sits at the intersection of educational psychology, cognitive science and motivational theory. Barry Zimmerman's self-regulated learning model — one of the most cited frameworks in educational psychology — identifies three essential capacities of high-performing students: goal setting, strategic self-monitoring, and self-evaluation. These capacities are not acquired incidentally; they require deliberate, guided development. Academic coaching is the practical delivery mechanism for this development. A 2019 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Educational Psychology (Dent and Koenka) found that self-regulation interventions produced statistically significant improvements in academic achievement across primary, secondary and tertiary education levels, with an average effect size of 0.48 — considered moderate-to-strong in education research. Importantly, the effects were largest for students who had previously underperformed relative to their measured ability — exactly the profile that prompts most families to seek coaching in the first place. 
## What to Look for When Choosing an Academic Coach
The term "academic coach" is unregulated, which means quality varies considerably. When evaluating a potential coach, the following questions separate substantive expertise from surface-level support: Do they have experience with students at international schools, specifically IB, A-Level or curriculum transition contexts? Can they articulate the difference between a metacognitive strategy and a study tip? How do they measure progress? What does a meaningful outcome look like after three months? How do they communicate with parents without breaching the student's trust in the coaching relationship? The most effective academic coaches combine a genuine understanding of adolescent development with practical familiarity with the specific academic systems their students navigate — including ManageBac, internal assessments and the particular pressure points of IB Year 1. ### What is an academic coach?
An academic coach is a specialist who teaches students how to learn — not what to learn. Rather than delivering subject content, they build learning strategies, time management systems and academic self-belief so the student can tackle any subject independently. 
### What is the difference between an academic coach and a private tutor?
A private tutor teaches the content of a specific subject. An academic coach builds the learning habits and systems that work across every subject — skills that last a lifetime, not just until the next test. 
### Is academic coaching useful for IB students?
Yes. The IB programme demands project management, analytical writing, long-term planning and strong self-regulation — exactly the areas academic coaching directly strengthens.

## What Is an International School?
An international school is a private school that delivers a globally recognised curriculum — such as IB, British IGCSE/A-Level, or American AP — independent of any single national education system. ## The Scale and Growth of International Education
International education is one of the world's fastest-growing sectors. As of 2024, the International Baccalaureate Organisation (IBO) authorises approximately 5,700 schools across 159 countries — up from 3,000 in 2010. The Council of International Schools (CIS) accredits over 1,200 institutions globally. This growth reflects structural demand: multinational mobility, the globalisation of university admissions, and parental awareness that national exam-based systems increasingly fail to develop the competencies required by leading employers and universities. For expat families specifically, international education represents a hedge against two domestic risks: the TL's long-run devaluation (which erodes the relative value of Turkish-system qualifications in global markets) and the Turkish education system's persistently low PISA rankings. Turkey's 2022 PISA scores placed it 40th out of 81 OECD and partner economies in mathematics — a result that has remained essentially flat for two consecutive cycles. Against this backdrop, the IB Diploma's recognition by over 5,700 schools and universities across 159 countries provides international students with a qualification whose value is genuinely global and not subject to exchange rate or geopolitical risk.

IBO research consistently shows that IB Diploma holders are admitted to selective universities at higher rates than the general applicant pool. A 2022 IBO study found that IB students in the United States were admitted to highly selective universities (those accepting fewer than 25% of applicants) at nearly twice the rate of non-IB applicants. In the UK, a disproportionate share of Oxford and Cambridge entrants hold IB Diplomas relative to A-Level holders at the same grade equivalent. For families with global university ambitions, this is not an abstract consideration — it is a measurable admission advantage. ### What does "international" mean?

The language of instruction is usually English and graduates can apply to universities worldwide. 
### What is the difference between an international school and a regular school?
Regular state schools follow a single country's national curriculum; international schools offer a global curriculum that provides pathways to universities in multiple countries. The student body is multinational, instruction is usually in English, and quality is assessed by independent accreditation bodies.

## [What Is EAL? English Support in Dubai Schools](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-eal/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/what-is-eal/  
**Date:** 2026-09-24

EAL — English as an Additional Language — is the name for the language support programmes that help non-native English speakers access the full curriculum in international schools. For expat families moving to Dubai, the question is almost always: "My child's English isn't strong enough — can they still go?" The answer is yes, and EAL is the reason why. This guide explains what EAL is, how Dubai schools deliver it, and what to look for when choosing a school for a non-native English speaker. 
## What Is EAL?
EAL stands for English as an Additional Language. It is the umbrella term for the support programmes that help students whose first language is not English develop the academic language skills they need to participate fully in school. International schools in Dubai are home to students from over 80 nationalities. The vast majority arrive with varying levels of English. EAL programmes are designed to meet this diversity — not to separate non-native speakers, but to give them the linguistic tools to access the same education as their peers. EAL is not private English tuition. Its goal is not simply to "teach English." It is to help a child develop the academic language needed to participate in science, maths, humanities and all other subjects — reading, writing, listening and speaking in an academic context. 
## EAL vs ESL: What's the Difference?
The two terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but they describe different things. 
### EAL vs ESL Comparison
ESL (English as a Second Language) Designed for students learning English from scratch. Often delivered through one-to-one or small-group sessions, sometimes by a teacher who speaks the child's first language. EAL (English as an Additional Language) Recognises that the child already has linguistic skills in one or more languages. Builds English on top of existing language capacity rather than treating the child as a blank slate. Better suited to multilingual cities like Dubai. Almost all international schools in Dubai use the EAL framework. For a Turkish child who may have some English from school in Turkey, or who already speaks Turkish and another language at home, EAL is the more accurate and more effective model. 
## How Is EAL Delivered in Dubai Schools?
Each school runs its own model, but three delivery approaches are common across KHDA-inspected schools: 
### 1. Pull-Out Support
The child leaves the main class for specific sessions — typically 3–5 hours per week — to work in a small EAL group. The most common starting model for newly arrived students. 
### 2. In-Class Support (Push-In)
An EAL specialist enters the main classroom and provides support during the lesson. The child stays with their peers, which accelerates social integration. Usually used once a child reaches intermediate level. 
### 3. Differentiated Instruction
The main class teacher adapts lessons for EAL learners — simplified reading materials, visual scaffolding, flexible assessment. The child progresses at their own pace within the mainstream classroom. The best schools use all three approaches in combination. A useful question to ask on a school visit: "How do you support EAL students within mainstream lessons?" If the answer only describes pull-out sessions, in-class support may be limited.

## How Long Does EAL Take?
This is the question families ask most. The honest answer is: it depends — but here are the practical benchmarks: 
### EAL Development Timeline
Basic social language 6–12 months. The child can hold conversations with peers, follow simple instructions, and participate in playground and classroom routines. Academic language proficiency 2–3 years. The ability to work independently in subjects like science, maths, and humanities. This stage takes the longest and is the most educationally critical. Exit from formal EAL support Based on school-defined assessment criteria; typically 1.5–3 years after entry. The student is considered to have reached mainstream class standards. Age makes a significant difference. Children aged 5–10 acquire language fastest — brain plasticity and social learning work together. Ages 11–14 progress at a moderate pace. For students aged 15 and above , the process takes longer and requires more targeted academic support alongside the EAL programme. 
## How Does KHDA Assess EAL?
In KHDA inspection reports, EAL provision is evaluated under the Inclusion and Personal Development headings. Inspectors ask: How well are EAL students integrated into mainstream lessons? Is language development tracked and documented over time? Do class teachers incorporate EAL needs into their lesson planning? Are exit criteria for the EAL programme clear and transparent? When reading a school's KHDA report, look for the EAL section under Inclusion. Phrases like "area for development" or "inconsistent support" in that section are worth questioning further before choosing the school. 
## 5 Questions to Ask About EAL When Visiting a School
"How do you assess EAL students on entry?" — A standardised assessment (e.g. WIDA, CAT4 language sub-test) is a strong indicator of a structured programme. "How many hours of EAL support per week?" — Fewer than 3 hours is thin; 5 hours or more is a solid starting point. "Are your EAL teachers qualified?" — Look for CELTA, Trinity TESOL or an equivalent international EAL qualification. "Are mainstream teachers trained in EAL strategies?" — EAL is not only the EAL teacher's responsibility; classroom teacher awareness is equally important. "What are your exit criteria?" — A clear, documented exit process signals that the programme has defined learning goals, not an open-ended dependency. 
## EAL for Turkish Children: Strengths and Challenges
Children coming from the Turkish education system typically arrive with strong academic foundations. Maths and science levels are often above Dubai class averages — which means that while language is developing, the child is not academically behind their peers. This is a significant advantage. The most common challenge is academic literacy : reading and writing in an academic register in English. Turkish is a highly phonetically regular language, so expat children can find English spelling and pronunciation patterns confusing at first. On the other hand, Turkish's complex grammar structure often accelerates the acquisition of English grammar, which is relatively straightforward by comparison. The stronger a child's Turkish literacy, the faster the EAL journey. Don't let Turkish slip — a strong first language is the foundation on which the second language is built most efficiently.

## [Why High Achievers Struggle with the IB](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/why-high-achievers-struggle-with-ib/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/why-high-achievers-struggle-with-ib/  
**Date:** 2026-10-01

1 October 2026 Ozlem Cimen 10 min read Updated: 3 October 2026 Summary The IB doesn't test intelligence — it tests time management and academic writing. Students from Turkey's exam-focused system are shaken by the Extended Essay, TOK and internal assessments. This post explains why, and how coaching solves it. 
# Why High-Achieving Turkish Students Struggle with the IB — And How Coaching Fixes It
IB programme Turkey IB extended essay help TOK essay support IB academic coaching "My child was one of the best students in Turkey. Since starting IB, it's as if they've forgotten everything." Working with IB students at TED Istanbul College and ENKA Schools for years, I heard this sentence more times than I can count. And every time, my answer was the same: the problem isn't intelligence — it's the system. The IB Diploma Programme demands a completely different cognitive infrastructure from what students in Turkey are used to. It doesn't test how much you've memorised; it tests whether you can think independently, manage a long-term project, and produce under pressure. 
## What Makes the IB Different?
What is the IB programme? The International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme is a two-year international upper secondary curriculum for students aged 16–19. It consists of 6 subject groups, the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS). It is recognised by more than 5,000 universities worldwide. Turkey's typical secondary system runs on a "work hard, score well, pass the exam" cycle — YKS preparation being its most concentrated form. The IB asks for a completely different skill set: Independent research — Questions come from the student, not the teacher Long-term project management — Deadlines stretch months ahead; planning is the student's responsibility Academic writing — Almost entirely absent from the Turkish curriculum Philosophical inquiry — TOK requires students to question the nature of knowledge itself These are habits, not intelligence. And they are not systematically built by the Turkish national curriculum. 
## 3 Critical Struggles: EE, TOK and Time Management

### 1. The Extended Essay
The Extended Essay is a 4,000-word independent research paper on a topic of the student's own choosing, completed with the guidance of a supervising teacher. It contributes directly to the IB Diploma score. It sounds manageable. In practice, it requires: Designing an original research question Sourcing and evaluating academic literature Constructing and writing a reasoned argument in academic English A months-long draft-revision cycle with a supervisor Managing all of this alongside 6 subjects, IA deadlines and TOK Why it breaks students: In Turkey, a student has never been asked to design a research question. The exam system provides every question; your job is to find the right answer. In the EE, you create the question — for most students, this is the first time in their academic life that this competency is demanded. 
### 2. Theory of Knowledge (TOK)
TOK is the IB's philosophical component — not a subject, but an inquiry framework that runs across all subjects. Students confront questions like: "How does knowledge in mathematics differ from knowledge in history?" "Does art actually produce knowledge?" "How do we know what we know?" TOK has two main submissions: TOK Essay — A 1,600-word analytical response to one of 6 prescribed questions set by the IB TOK Exhibition — A visual/written presentation connecting 3 objects to a knowledge question For students from Turkey, TOK typically begins at "I don't even understand what's being asked." Abstract, cross-disciplinary thinking of this kind is not systematically developed in the Turkish curriculum. A misunderstood TOK essay can significantly damage the overall diploma score. 
### 3. Internal Assessments (IAs) and Time Management
Every one of the 6 subjects includes at least one Internal Assessment (IA) : lab reports, oral assessments, research papers, artistic portfolios. That is 6 IAs + Extended Essay + TOK — each on a different schedule, in a different format. The school provides the timeline. But no teacher has the individual time to help each student build their own personal plan. The result: most IB students encounter their first last-minute crisis in Year 1, and repeat it in Year 2. 
## Why School Can't Fill This Gap
This is a question I hear from dozens of IB parents: "The school is an IB school — shouldn't they be providing this support?" IB schools deliver the curriculum — content is taught, deadlines are announced. But providing EE supervision to 20 students simultaneously, tracking each student's individual IA calendar, or running personal TOK inquiry sessions is not structurally possible in a classroom setting. The issue isn't school quality — it's a structural reality: one-to-one accountability and a personalised roadmap cannot be delivered in a classroom. 
## The Coaching Difference: A Personalised IB Roadmap
IB coaching doesn't teach content. It does this instead: What IB academic coaching covers: — Guidance on EE topic selection and research question design — Building the TOK essay structure and argument framework together — Creating a personal timeline integrating IA, EE and TOK deadlines — Weekly check-in sessions to maintain consistency and motivation — Exam period strategy: which subject gets how much time, in which order Working with someone who knows both the inside of the IB and the specific points where international students stumble turns that "everything piled on at once" feeling into "I have a plan." I don't teach subjects in the IB. I teach students how to carry two years.

## [Why the Turkish Education System Falls Short](https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/why-turkish-education-falls-short/)

**URL:** https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/why-turkish-education-falls-short/  
**Date:** 2026-06-12

12 June 2026 Ozlem Cimen 10 min read Updated: 2 October 2026 Summary A data-driven analysis of why Turkey's education system falls short of global standards — examining PISA rankings, rote-learning culture, frequent curriculum overhauls, and the persistent English language gap. 
# Why the Turkish Education System Falls Short:

# Observations from an Expat Mother
Turkish education system PISA Turkey results international school gap Turkish expat education rote learning system A mother I worked with told me that on her daughter's first day at an international school in America, the teacher asked her a simple question: "What do you think about this?" The child froze. She had spent years as a student in Turkey, trying in every class to find the one correct answer. But "what do you think?" was different. The question caught her completely off guard — because in the Turkish education system, that question is rarely asked. When I spoke with the mother, we both noticed the same thing: she believed she had raised her daughter well, but she had unknowingly prepared her for the wrong race. I've heard this story countless times. Different cities, different schools — from Dubai, from London, from Singapore. But the same shock, the same moment. Today I want to talk about why that shock happens, and why the Turkish education system falls behind international standards — not emotionally, but with data. 
## What Do the PISA Numbers Say?
Turkey has participated regularly in the OECD's PISA assessments since 2003. And since 2003, it has never once reached the OECD average in any assessment cycle. Mathematics, science and reading literacy — consistently below average in all three core domains. According to the 2022 PISA results, Turkey ranks below 40th out of 81 countries in mathematics. A more concrete statistic: a significant proportion of 15-year-old students in Turkey can't even demonstrate the minimum proficiency level in mathematical literacy. This isn't just a test-score issue — it's an objective indicator of how prepared children actually are for real life. So why does this happen? There are five core reasons. 
## 1. A Curriculum Built on Memorisation
Memorisation still sits at the centre of education in Turkey. Finding the correct answer is valued far more than understanding how you arrived at it. Classroom discussion, critical questioning, being able to say "I think" — these remain a matter of an individual teacher's preference, not something the curriculum is designed around. International education systems take a fundamentally different approach. In America, students encounter a method that moves from concrete to pictorial to abstract. Fewer topics, deeper understanding. A child isn't asked to "memorise this formula" but to answer "how — and why — would you solve this problem?" The IB (International Baccalaureate) curriculum pushes this even further. Inquiry, reflection and ethical questioning aren't extracurricular add-ons — they're the core of the curriculum. Ozlem Cimen — A Note from the Field A child I worked with solved a maths problem his own way in his American school and presented it to the class for the first time — and the teacher said "what a great approach," even though the answer was wrong. His mother told me, astonished: "In Turkey, that answer would have cost him points." 
## 2. 17 System Overhauls in 20 Years
Turkey's education system has undergone 17 major overhauls in the past 20 years. Nine different Ministers of National Education have come and gone. Each minister introduced a new model, a new exam, a new curriculum. This instability doesn't just affect parents — it cuts deep into teachers as well. The topics you taught one year disappear from the curriculum the next. The lesson plans you built five years ago are obsolete today. Teacher motivation, professional confidence and long-term learning planning all take the hit from this constant churn. Compare this to Finland. Finland's education system consistently ranks at the very top of PISA. Teachers there hold master's degrees, enjoy professional autonomy, and trust the system. Change is slow, deliberate and consistent. In Finland, even the debate over an education reform plays out over a decade-long process. Turkish families who've relocated abroad see this very clearly. What they all tend to say is similar: "Schools here are planning ten years ahead. The system in Turkey sometimes can't even plan next year." 
## 3. Exam Pressure Overrides Everything Else
In Turkey, a child's school life revolves around specific exams: LGS, YKS. Spending on private tutoring and prep courses to prepare for these exams runs into the billions of lira nationwide. According to TÜİK data, private tutoring and prep-course spending remains the fastest-growing line item in Turkish families' education budgets. And the result? Children burn through their weekends, their sleep patterns break down, their curiosity gets ground away. They go to school to pass exams, not to learn. Yet in modern education approaches, the exam is a tool, not the goal. Finland has no standardised tests. Assessment is used to track a student's development — not to rank them. The result? Finnish students grow up with less stress and higher learning motivation, and have topped the PISA rankings for years. I see the same striking contrast in international schools in Dubai and London. The children in front of me want to "finish the project," not "study for the exam." The way they engage with education is fundamentally different. 
## 4. The English and Global Competency Gap
The shock I hear most often from Turkish families who've relocated abroad is this: "My child's English was so much further behind than I thought." English instruction exists in Turkey — but it's largely passive. Knowing grammar rules is very different from thinking and speaking in that language. The average Turkish high school graduate's active English usage skill, according to the EF English Proficiency Index, lags well behind Europe. Turkey sits in the "low proficiency" category on that index. In international schools, English isn't a subject — it's the language of thinking, writing and being. The children of families I work with arrive abroad knowing English but unable to think in English . They can build an equation in English, but they can't defend an idea in English. Closing this gap takes time — and with the right support, it happens far faster. The most critical academic English skills are: Academic writing Argument development Source evaluation None of these are taught systematically in the Turkish curriculum. 
## 5. The Socioeconomic Divide Splits Education in Two
Which school you attend in Turkey is determined to a large extent by your family's income level. The gap between a state school and a good private school is chasm-sized — in physical infrastructure, in teacher quality, and in the opportunities offered to students. OECD data puts a number on this: in Turkey, socioeconomic status affects student achievement at a rate far above the OECD average. In other words, which family you're born into determines what you learn in Turkey. This is an education-equity problem — and at the same time, a global-competitiveness problem. In modern education systems — Finland, Canada, New Zealand — this gap is far narrower. State schools are genuinely competitive; the private-school advantage isn't nearly as decisive. 
## It's Not Just Turkey
I want to stress an important nuance here. Critiquing the Turkish education system isn't the same as dismissing it entirely. There are genuinely good teachers and genuinely strong schools in Turkey. And the system has made meaningful progress in PISA since 2003 — its starting point was far lower. But the pace of progress isn't enough. And for families relocating abroad, or aiming for a global education for their child, the issue is this: the gap with the international system is still wide. Knowing this gap, accepting it, and preparing accordingly — that's what turns the transition into a success. 
## Getting Ready for "What Do You Think?"
That mother's daughter is now one of the top students at the same school. What made the difference? Managing the transition correctly. The right school, the right academic support, the right adaptation guidance. Moving from Turkish education to an international system — especially IB, A-Level or the American curriculum — requires serious preparation. Skipping that preparation and assuming "I'll just find a good school, the child will figure out the rest" is exactly how you end up as that frozen child. But with the right support, this transition becomes far smoother and far faster. I've seen it happen, over and over, with dozens of families. 👉 If you're planning to relocate abroad or looking for the right school for your child, get in touch for a free consultation. ## The Most Common Questions from Turkish Families

### Where does Turkey rank in PISA?
In the 2022 assessment, Turkey ranked clearly below the OECD average in mathematics and reading literacy, out of 81 countries. 
### How many times has the Ministry of Education curriculum changed?
More than 17 major overhauls in the past 20 years. These frequent changes create serious instability for both students and teachers. 
### Is moving from Turkish education to an international school difficult?
It requires serious adjustment, particularly in academic English, critical thinking and project-based learning. Professional consulting significantly eases this transition. 
### Can a Turkish high school diploma get you into a university abroad?
Most target universities require an internationally standardised exam result such as SAT/ACT, A-Level or IB. Options with only a Turkish diploma are quite limited. ### My Child Is Starting an International School: 5 Critical Mistakes to Avoid
URL: https://www.edualist.com/en/blog/child-starting-international-school-dubai/
Tarih: 2026-10-03
Özet: Getting into an international school and succeeding in one are different skills. Five mistakes: (1) treating transition as logistics not a management-skills problem — test independent project capability first; (2) assuming English level is sufficient — conversational vs academic English differ, ask school about EAL support; (3) not measuring academic level before transition — use EduEntry or CAT4 to identify gaps; (4) importing old "success" definition — IB uses 7-point scale, 5–6 is good; (5) leaving first year unsupported across academic, social and identity dimensions. First-term checklist: assessment 2–3 months before, EAL contact 1–2 months before, coach first session before school starts, no grade pressure in month 1, weekly emotional check-ins, end-of-term review with coach. ### Dubai'de Okul Seçerken Yapılan 5 Hata

Tarih: 2026-10-18
Özet: Türkiye'den Dubai'ye taşınan ailelerin okul seçimi ve başvuru sürecinde en sık yaptığı 5 hata. (1) "Taşınınca bakarız" demek — Outstanding okullar 12–24 ay bekleme, taşınma kararıyla aynı anda araştırma başlamalı. (2) WhatsApp grubuna göre okul seçmek — sürü etkisi gerçek, profil eşleşmesi topluluk baskısından önce gelir. (3) KHDA Outstanding'i tek kriter saymak — EAL desteği, sınıf büyüklüğü, öğretmen sirkülasyonu, kampüs kültürü KHDA raporuna yansımaz. (4) Müfredatı es geçmek — IB analitik/öz-yönetim, A-Level derinlemesine konu odaklı, AP geniş yük+SAT; müfredat seçimi okul adından önce gelir. (5) Lokasyonu son kriter bırakmak — önce okul listesi, sonra okulların yakınındaki semtler; yanlış semt = günlük 40–60 dk yol. Her hata için pratik çözüm adımı ve ilgili yazıya mini bağlantı. Sonda 5 adımlı doğru okul seçim çerçevesi. CTA: ortada ve sonda ücretsiz 30 dk keşif görüşmesi.

### Dubai 2027-2028 Okul Başvuru Takvimi: Ekim'de Ne Yapmalısınız?
URL: https://www.edualist.com/blog/dubai-okul-basvuru-takvimi-2027/
Tarih: 2026-10-18
Özet: Ekim 2026 itibarıyla KHDA Outstanding okullar için 2027-2028 başvuru durumu: Repton (10–16 ay bekleme → Eylül 2027 için hâlâ zamanında), GEMS Wellington ve Nord Anglia (12–18 ay → sınırda, hemen başvurun), JESS (12–24 ay → bekleme listesi ihtimali yüksek), DIA Emirates Hills (18–24 ay → Eylül 2027 için geç, 2028 hedefleyin). Okul tipine göre takvim tablosu: Outstanding için hemen başvuru, Very Good için Ara 2026–Şub 2027, Good için Mar–May 2027. Gerekli belgeler: son 2 yılın karneleri (İngilizce çevirili), pasaport, aşı kartı, referans mektubu. 3 kritik hata: tek okula başvurmak, belgeleri ertelemek, lokasyonu göz ardı etmek. Yazı orta ve sonunda ücretsiz 30 dk keşif görüşmesi CTA'sı.

### Dubai'de Lise Seçimi: IB Diploma mı, A-Level mı? Müfredat ve Okul Rehberi 2026
URL: https://www.edualist.com/blog/dubai-lise-secimi/
Tarih: 2026-10-19
Özet: Dubai lisesi (Year 10–13) için müfredat seçim rehberi. British sistemde lise = Year 10–11 GCSE/IGCSE + Year 12–13 A-Level veya IB Diploma. IB Diploma: 6 ders + EE + TOK + CAS, geniş kapsam, global üniversite (ABD, Hollanda, Kanada, Almanya, Türkiye) açısından güçlü. A-Level: 3-4 derste derinleşme, İngiltere ve Commonwealth üniversiteleri için geleneksel tercih. Okul tablosu: DIA Emirates Hills (tam IB, 70K–105K AED), Repton (A-Level, 65K–85K AED), JESS (A-Level, 55K–78K AED), GEMS Wellington (A-Level, 65K–98K AED), Nord Anglia (IB Diploma seçeneği, 55K–92K AED), Dubai College (A-Level, 60K–80K AED), Kings School (A-Level, 55K–80K AED), Dubai American Academy (AP+IB, 55K–85K AED). Türk aileler için kritik notlar: akademik İngilizce hazırlığı, EAL desteği farkları, üniversite danışmanlığı altyapısı. Başvuru zamanlaması: Year 10 için Year 8–9'da, Year 12 için okulun ayrı kabul süreci. Yaygın yanılgılar: IB daha prestijli değil, A-Level daha kolay değil.

### Repton, GEMS Wellington, Nord Anglia ve JESS Karşılaştırması 2026
URL: https://www.edualist.com/blog/dubai-okul-karsilastirma/
Tarih: 2026-10-17
Özet: Dubai'nin en sık sorulan dört okulu — Repton, GEMS Wellington, Nord Anglia, JESS ve IB için DIA — Türk aile perspektifinden detaylı karşılaştırma. Tamamı KHDA Outstanding. Repton (70k–85k AED, İngiliz, akademik disiplin, Nad Al Sheba), GEMS Wellington (57k–98k AED, İngiliz, büyük kampüs, çok uluslu), Nord Anglia (50k–92k AED, İngiliz+IB, sanat ve proje odaklı), JESS (48k–78k AED, İngiliz, Türk aileler arasında en yaygın), DIA (65k–95k AED, tam IB continuum). Her okul için: güçlü yönler, dikkat noktaları ve hangi çocuk profiline uyduğu.
